author: Fowler
title: Task-specific Filtering for Layer-wise Knowledge Transfer in Language Model Compression
abstract: Transferring knowledge from a teacher model to a smaller student model by matching hidden features at each intermediate layer has proven effective for reducing language model size. In this process, the student aims to replicate the internal representations of the teacher throughout the network. Nonetheless, this type of layer-wise distillation presents difficulties: limited student capacity often leads to insufficient model fitting, and the teacher's internal features may include unnecessary content for the actual application. To tackle these issues, the proposed method introduces task-specific filters that, at every layer, selectively align the student's and teacher's representations, retaining information crucial for the target objective. This approach narrows the discrepancy between teacher and student, enhancing student adaptation to the task requirements. The method is assessed under both continual pre-training and fine-tuning regimes, showing clear and reliable gains compared with other distillation approaches in each case.

author: Johnson
title: Addressing Gender Disparity in Distilled Language Models Through Counterfactual Reassignment Procedures
abstract: Text generation by language models achieves high fluency, and compression methods like knowledge distillation make deployment feasible in low-resource environments. Despite these advantages, such models often display various biases, notably by incorrectly linking gender-neutral occupations to a specific gender. Absent any fairness interventions, distillation processes risk retaining or amplifying these biases from the teacher model in the produced student model. To address this, this work introduces a new strategy for reducing gender bias in generated text by enforcing fairness during knowledge distillation. The proposed method incorporates two key changes to standard distillation: first, it alters the teacher's probability outputs via counterfactual role reversal; second, it enriches the training data accordingly. Assessment of gender polarity among occupational terms appears in generated outputs from distilled and finetuned GPT-2 variants, showing marked decreases in gender bias with negligible detriment to model performance. Nevertheless, experiments reveal that decreasing gender polarity in language generation does not correspond to gains in fairness for learned representations or downstream classification tasks.

author: Hill
title: Hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning for Lifelong Knowledge Transfer in Minecraft
abstract: This work introduces a framework for lifelong learning that supports both retention of acquired knowledge over time and effective transfer of skills across tasks. To address the lifelong learning challenges presented by Minecraft—a widely used, complex, and unsolved environment—our approach involves developing reusable skills called Deep Skill Networks. These are integrated within a hierarchical deep reinforcement learning architecture through two main mechanisms: first, by assembling a deep skill array, and second, by utilizing a skill distillation process, which is our adaptation of policy distillation (Rusu et al. 2015) to the context of skill acquisition. The skill distillation strategy permits the hierarchical model to efficiently preserve earlier knowledge, aggregate several reusable skills, and consolidate them within a single distilled network. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed hierarchical model achieves better results and requires fewer training samples than a standard Deep Q Network (Mnih et al. 2015) on various Minecraft sub-tasks.

author: Walker
title: A Meta Learning-Based Approach for Adaptive Teacher Models in Knowledge Distillation
abstract: This work introduces a knowledge distillation approach employing meta learning, where the teacher network is trained to optimize its ability to transfer knowledge, instead of remaining static during student model training. Within this meta learning-based distillation framework, the teacher network leverages feedback derived from the performance of the student network to enhance its guidance capabilities. Additionally, a pilot update strategy is proposed to strengthen the synchronization between the inner-learner and meta-learner, particularly in meta learning settings aimed at advancing the inner-learner. Experimental evaluation across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrates that the proposed method achieves notable gains over standard knowledge distillation techniques, and demonstrates reduced sensitivity to student model size and hyperparameter selections, thus broadening the applicability of knowledge distillation across architectures and tasks.

author: Doyle
title: A Knowledge Distillation Approach for Recommender Systems Utilizing Expert Transfer and Relaxed Ranking
abstract: Knowledge distillation, in which a complex teacher model conveys its knowledge to a simpler student model, has become increasingly prevalent in recent recommender systems as a means to decrease inference time without substantial sacrifice in effectiveness. Existing leading approaches to knowledge distillation in this context have primarily centered on encouraging the student model to closely replicate the outputs of the teacher model, but this ignores much of the information embedded within the teacher. To address this gap, we introduce a new knowledge distillation strategy specifically designed for recommender systems that allows the student to benefit from both the internal knowledge representations of the teacher and its output predictions. The approach comprises two key components: (1) a Distillation Experts mechanism, which leverages selected experts and an expert selection mechanism to directly impart portions of the teacher’s internal knowledge to the student, overcoming the student’s limited capacity, and (2) a Relaxed Ranking Distillation step, which communicates the information contained in the teacher’s predictive output by considering partial ranking agreements among items. Comprehensive experimental results demonstrate that this proposed framework achieves better results than existing strong baselines and can match or exceed the original teacher’s predictive capability, all while offering more efficient inference.

author: Rhodes
title: Continual Language Knowledge Transfer via Teacher-Student Distillation
abstract: Maintaining stable performance in lifelong language learning across sequential tasks, without incurring the drops typically observed relative to multi-task models, remains a significant challenge. In response, this work introduces a straightforward and effective strategy for alleviating such degradation, which can be integrated with existing lifelong language learning frameworks. The approach involves having a teacher model first acquire the new task, then transferring its expertise to the lifelong language learner through knowledge distillation during the training on each additional task. This enables the learner to assimilate novel information while retaining mastery of preceding tasks. Empirical results indicate that employing the described method reliably enhances the capabilities of earlier leading systems, substantially reducing the gap in performance with respect to multi-task approaches on both sequence generation and text classification benchmarks.

author: Mcclain
title: Transferring Internal Representations During Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Commonly, knowledge distillation involves training a compact student model to replicate the behavior of a larger teacher model, with the aim of compressing information by guiding the student using the output probabilities (soft-labels) produced by the teacher. While this approach targets efficient transfer of knowledge, significant disparities in model capacity can result in the student's internal representations deviating from those of the teacher, even if its outputs closely follow the soft-labels. Such divergence may negatively affect the student's ability to generalize as intended. This study introduces a methodology for distilling the internal representations learned by a large architecture like BERT to a less complex counterpart. Two distinct techniques for this internal representation transfer are defined, along with several algorithmic strategies for implementing the distillation process. Through experiments on multiple GLUE benchmark tasks, we provide consistent evidence that supplementing soft-label distillation with internal representation distillation yields better performance than relying on soft-labels alone.

author: Miller
title: Enhancing Spoken Question Answering Accuracy through a Distillation Approach
abstract: Spoken question answering tasks often involve intricate spoken material that the system must interpret. The process of automatic speech recognition (ASR) significantly impacts the construction of QA models. Nonetheless, existing research indicates that ASR frequently creates transcripts with considerable noise, which substantially hampers machine understanding in SQA scenarios. To confront this challenge, the proposed method introduces a new distillation-based training paradigm. This involves applying knowledge distillation between spoken documents and their text-based equivalents. The primary contribution of this study is the use of supervision derived from the language model to mitigate discrepancies between automatic and human-produced transcripts, thereby boosting student model accuracy. Experimental findings show that this methodology achieves superior results compared to multiple competitive language model baselines when evaluated on the Spoken-SQuAD benchmark.

author: Henderson
title: Ensemble Compression Using Adversarial Knowledge Transfer Across Multiple Models
abstract: Top-performing deep neural systems frequently rely on ensembles comprising several independent networks. However, practical deployment with extensive test sets, like those in ImageNet, is hindered by the prohibitively large memory consumption and slow inference speed required by such combined models. Here, we describe a procedure to merge the predictive power of multiple separately trained deep neural networks (teachers) into a single compact network (student) via knowledge distillation. This process leverages an adversarial learning framework: student training incorporates a loss function structured by blocks, which simultaneously steers the student toward capturing teacher-derived representations and drives a discriminator to discern between outputs generated by teachers and the student. Notable merits of the introduced approach are as follows: (1) the student network, trained with the assistance of discriminators, attains improvements in optimization relative to its original counterpart; (2) a single forward computation achieves rapid classification, while surpassing conventional ensembles consisting of the initial independent models; (3) the student is capable of absorbing knowledge distilled from teacher architectures of varying types. Comprehensive experimentation across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, and ImageNet benchmarks substantiates the value of this methodology. Specifically, applying the method to ResNet-50 on ImageNet results in validation top-1 and top-5 errors of 21.79% and 5.99%, thereby outperforming the original network by 2.06% and 1.14%, respectively. Source code and pre-trained models are hosted at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

author: Robinson
title: Optimizing Teacher Models for Enhanced Knowledge Distillation to Students
abstract: This work introduces a new strategy for knowledge distillation, which emphasizes transferring dark knowledge by designing teacher models intended to better assist student learning. Diverging from prevalent approaches that focus on training student models from fixed pretrained teachers, our method specifically trains teacher networks to yield student-optimized representations, achieved by integrating student branches during teacher model optimization. Since our central innovation concerns the process for training teacher networks and the standard knowledge distillation step that follows remains uncomplicated, this approach can serve as an improvement to many existing distillation frameworks, helping diverse student models achieve higher accuracy and faster convergence. Experimental results show that our method significantly boosts performance for a variety of established knowledge distillation techniques, across multiple teacher-student model pairs, including settings with heterogeneous architectures and scenarios where student model details are unavailable when optimizing teacher networks.

author: Wagner
title: A Method for Leveraging Soft Target Probabilities from the Training Model Itself in NLP Applications
abstract: With the increasing dominance of deep learning in natural language processing (NLP), neural models have achieved strong results across a range of tasks, sometimes exceeding human baselines. This success is largely attributable to the effective way deep learning models capture and utilize knowledge. Although numerous strategies have aimed at modeling representations more efficiently, knowledge distillation—often relying on pretrained deep networks—demonstrates that soft target probabilities can aid the training of additional neural architectures. Here, we introduce a novel form of knowledge distillation, termed the proposed method, which utilizes the training model’s own soft target probabilities. In this approach, information with multiple modes is extracted from the word embedding representations located directly beneath the softmax function. To address computational demands, the proposed method makes an approximation of these soft target probabilities. We present experiments applying this technique to core NLP tasks, specifically language modeling and neural machine translation. The outcomes indicate that the approach described here enhances task performance.

author: Johnson
title: Theoretical Analysis of Knowledge Distillation in Overparameterized Neural Architectures: Transfer Risk, Sample Utilization, and Non-Ideal Teacher Effects
abstract: In the framework of knowledge distillation, a student model is trained by leveraging the softened outputs (logits) generated by a teacher network. This technique has proven to be effective for compressing models and transferring learned information. Despite its empirical success, a comprehensive theoretical explanation remains underdeveloped. Meanwhile, developments in understanding the neural tangent kernel have made it feasible to represent very wide neural networks using linearized models defined by their random feature mappings. This study investigates knowledge distillation applied to wide neural networks from a theoretical perspective. Initially, we derive a transfer risk bound for the linear approximation of such networks. Next, we introduce an indicator of the challenge inherent to a specific learning task, termed data inefficiency. Utilizing this measure, we demonstrate that when the teacher is optimal, providing a greater proportion of soft labels from the teacher may offer advantages. In addition, we analyze the situation where the teacher's outputs are imperfect, and observe that incorporating hard labels assists in correcting inaccuracies in the teacher's guidance, thereby shedding light on why combining hard and soft labels is effective in practice.

author: Gonzalez
title: Progressive Guidance: Using Dual Teachers in Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Deploying deep neural networks on devices with limited computational and storage capabilities is hindered by their high requirements. The aim of knowledge distillation is to enable a smaller student model to acquire knowledge from a more complex, pre-trained teacher. Yet, standard approaches in this area often neglect the informative dynamics present during the training process in relation to final outcomes. To address this, this study introduces a novel knowledge distillation technique involving two distinct teacher models. The first, initialized without prior training (referred to here as the scratch teacher), facilitates incremental learning by providing its intermediate outputs to the student, encouraging the student to follow a more effective progression toward accurate final logits. The second, a pre-trained teacher (the expert teacher), directs the student’s attention toward regions in the feature space that are especially beneficial for the given task. By integrating the guidance from these two types of teachers, significant improvements in student model performance are observed. Experimental results on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, and Tiny ImageNet datasets demonstrate that the described method is both effective and achieves outcomes matching or exceeding current best-performing techniques.

author: Santos
title: Channel-Based Attention Mechanism Applied to Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Transferring learned information from a teacher model to a student model, known as knowledge distillation, aims to enable the student to achieve nearly equivalent accuracy to the teacher but with reduced model size and computational requirements. This work introduces a novel distillation framework, incorporating two distinct transfer strategies alongside a mechanism for progressively reducing the influence of the distillation loss. The initial strategy makes use of attention mechanisms specific to channels, facilitating the passage of channel-level representations from the teacher to the student. The second strategy, termed here as Guided Knowledge Distillation, limits the student's learning to only the accurate outputs of the teacher, in contrast to standard methods where the student is trained to reproduce the teacher’s entire output distribution for every example. Additionally, an approach referred to as Early Decay Teacher gradually diminishes the effect of the teacher-supervised loss over time, allowing the student to assume greater control of the training process. Experiments are performed on the ImageNet and CIFAR100 datasets. On the ImageNet benchmark, the approach achieves a top-1 error rate of 27.68% with a ResNet18 student, surpassing leading prior techniques. Notably, on CIFAR100, results indicate the student model exceeds the teacher's performance. Implementation details and code are available at https://github.com/zhouzaida/channel-distillation.

author: Gardner
title: Transferring Adversarial Robustness in Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Knowledge distillation yields compact neural networks with strong classification ability, yet these reduced models often exhibit susceptibility to adversarial perturbations. Here, we investigate the process by which adversarial robustness is conveyed from teacher to student during distillation. Our results reveal that substantial robustness can be passed to student models, even when only non-adversarial samples are used in distillation. We further present a method for enhancing student network robustness by modeling the distillation process to explicitly transfer the teacher's resilience to adversarial attacks. This approach not only matches standard distillation in producing compact, accurate models, but also endows student models with the robust characteristics of their larger counterparts. Empirically, student models generated using our approach significantly exceed the adversarial robustness of similarly structured networks that undergo standard adversarial training, achieving performance beyond current leading techniques on widely used robustness evaluation datasets. Additionally, we incorporate recent advances in rapid adversarial training to accelerate the robust distillation procedure.

author: Robinson
title: A Formal Examination of Ensemble Methods, Knowledge Distillation, and Self-Distillation in Deep Neural Networks
abstract: This work provides a formal analysis of how combining outputs from multiple deep neural networks as an ensemble enhances test accuracy, and investigates the process by which this increased performance can be transferred to an individual model using knowledge distillation. Focusing on the specific and nontrivial scenario where each network in the ensemble is independently initialized, shares the identical architecture, follows the same training procedures, and is trained on the same dataset—differentiated solely by distinct random seeds—we demonstrate that the phenomena observed with ensembles and knowledge distillation in deep learning contrast starkly with classical learning theory results, including those involving boosting and neural tangent kernels (NTKs). To address this, we introduce a theoretical framework establishing that, under a particular data condition termed 'multi-view', a collection of independently optimized neural networks can rigorously be shown to boost test accuracy through ensembling, and furthermore, that it is possible to theoretically guarantee the transmission of this enhanced accuracy to a single student model by training it to predict the ensemble’s outputs rather than the ground-truth labels. Our findings clarify that the mechanisms behind ensemble performance in deep learning diverge fundamentally from established theory, emphasizing the role of 'dark knowledge'—intricate information embedded in the ensemble’s predictions—which is leveraged during distillation. Finally, we show self-distillation may be interpreted as an implicit strategy that unites ensemble averaging with knowledge distillation, thereby yielding test accuracy improvements.

author: Lawrence
title: Transferring Knowledge from a Deep Pose Regression Network for Compact Visual Odometry
abstract: We introduce a new approach for transferring knowledge from a deep pose regressor network to enhance the efficiency of Visual Odometry (VO) systems. Classical distillation methods utilize 'dark knowledge' for effective knowledge transfer, but such information is absent in pose regression tasks and the teacher’s outputs may not consistently be reliable. In this work, we address this by conditioning the strength of knowledge transfer on the degree of confidence in the teacher’s outputs, using the teacher loss to compute a confidence measure that adaptively modulates the influence of the teacher’s prediction. This confidence-guided weighting is integrated both into the main training objective through an Attentive Imitation Loss (AIL), and into the training of intermediate feature representations using an Attentive Hint Training (AHT) strategy. As far as we know, this is the first demonstration of successful knowledge distillation from a deep network specialized in pose regression. Experiments on the KITTI and Malaga datasets indicate the student model can maintain predictions close to those of the teacher, while achieving up to 92.95% reduction in the number of parameters and improving computational speed by a factor of 2.12.

author: Pacheco
title: Enhancing Knowledge Distillation Using Adversarial Examples Emphasizing Classifier Boundaries
abstract: Approaches for knowledge distillation have lately enabled the transfer of representations from a pre-trained teacher to a student network to facilitate improved student learning, yet identifying an optimal distillation strategy remains unresolved. This study introduces an alternative angle focusing on the decision boundary, a crucial factor in classifier design. Since the effectiveness of a classifier's generalization is strongly tied to the quality of its decision boundary, leveraging information closely tied to this boundary is likely beneficial for knowledge distillation. To accomplish this, adversarial attack methods are employed to extract examples that are pivotal for defining the decision boundary. The method presented here builds on this, systematically instructing the student network through training on adversarial samples that reveal the decision boundary. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that this approach produces enhanced knowledge transfer, with results that reach current state-of-the-art benchmarks.

author: Smith
title: Interpreting Knowledge Distillation Through Quantitative Analysis of Encoded Knowledge
abstract: We introduce a framework to elucidate why knowledge distillation is effective by measuring and assessing the presence of both task-related and unrelated visual concepts represented within the intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN). We put forward three main hypotheses: (1) models trained by distillation acquire a greater number of visual concepts than models trained solely on original data; (2) knowledge distillation encourages simultaneous acquisition of a diverse set of visual concepts in the DNN, in contrast to the sequential concept acquisition observed when training with raw data alone; and (3) optimization trajectories during training with distillation are more consistent compared to those emerging from direct data-driven training. To address these, we develop three quantitative approaches to analyze the feature representations inside the network. Experimental validation on multiple neural architectures supports all proposed hypotheses.

author: Shaffer
title: Sample Selection Strategies in Knowledge Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
abstract: Neural Machine Translation systems have advanced state-of-the-art results across multiple translation datasets. Knowledge distillation, a significant area in NMT research, improves model effectiveness by passing knowledge from the teacher model to the student across individual training instances. Despite its prevalence, how different training samples influence and relate to each other as conduits for this knowledge transfer has been largely unexplored. This study introduces a new framework enabling thorough assessment of differential sample influence by contrasting partitions of the training data. Leveraging this framework, our comprehensive experiments reveal that providing the student with more teacher knowledge is not always beneficial; utilizing teacher outputs for certain samples can actually degrade the overall effectiveness of distillation. To mitigate these challenges, we devise two straightforward but efficient methods, performed either at the batch level or across the entire training set, to identify which samples should be selected for the distillation process. We validate these sample selection techniques on the large-scale WMT'14 English-to-German and WMT'19 Chinese-to-English translation tasks. Our results demonstrate that the proposed sample selection leads to performance gains of up to +1.28 BLEU for English-to-German and +0.89 BLEU for Chinese-to-English over a Transformer baseline.

author: Wolfe
title: Resource-Conserving and Reliable Data-Free Knowledge Distillation through Generative Replay Mechanisms
abstract: Transferring knowledge from a pre-trained teacher neural network to a student model without utilizing the original dataset is achievable with Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (KD). Common techniques involve employing a validation set to track student accuracy on real data and select the model state with the highest observed performance. Yet, in real-world scenarios, access to validation data during distillation may also be absent, rendering it impossible to capture the optimal student model checkpoint. To address this limitation, a desirable data-free KD process must maintain resilience and, preferably, produce consistent improvements in student accuracy throughout training. This is complicated by degradation in student knowledge that arises from shifts in the distributions of generated datasets. While maintaining and replaying synthetic examples can counteract this degradation, such a strategy necessitates additional memory resources and may pose privacy risks. The proposed method addresses this by learning the distribution of previously encountered synthetic examples using a generative model. Specifically, a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) is constructed and trained with a specially designed objective to best capture the representations of the synthetic data. The generative replay mechanism enables the student to revisit informative samples produced by the VAE, circumventing the need for explicit sample storage and preventing deterioration of learned knowledge. Evaluations conducted on standard image classification datasets indicate that this technique consistently maximizes the expected accuracy of the distilled model while avoiding the significant memory demands associated with sample-saving approaches.

author: Peterson
title: Investigating the Role of Knowledge Distillation in Non-autoregressive Sequence Generation for Machine Translation
abstract: Non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) approaches generate the entire output token sequence concurrently, resulting in significant boosts to inference efficiency over autoregressive baselines. Most current NAT frameworks utilize knowledge distillation, in which a pretrained autoregressive model supplies training data, leading to enhanced outcomes. While knowledge distillation has been shown empirically to yield notable accuracy improvements for NAT, its underlying efficacy was not previously well understood. This study introduces controlled experiments specifically devised to determine the underlying factors making distillation essential in NAT training. The analysis demonstrates that knowledge distillation serves to lower data complexity and assists NAT systems in capturing output variability. The experiments also reveal a close association between a NAT model’s expressiveness and the ideal level of distilled data complexity that yields optimal translation results. Building on these insights, the work presents methods for modifying data complexity to further enhance NAT performance. Leveraging these strategies, our models reach state-of-the-art accuracy for NAT architectures and substantially reduce the performance differential with autoregressive models on the WMT14 English-German task.

author: Moore
title: Attention-Driven Feature Alignment for Knowledge Distillation Without Manual Link Selection
abstract: Knowledge distillation leverages a pre-trained teacher model’s general representations to supervise a student network. Traditional approaches frequently impose correspondences between intermediate features in the teacher and student networks via manual configuration, relying on pre-established mappings to convey information. Such manual determination is prone to constructing suboptimal connections, which in turn restrains distillation gains. While previous work has made efforts to overcome this, reliably establishing beneficial associations remains complex in applied contexts. Here, we propose a new distillation technique that harnesses every feature layer in the teacher network, eliminating the need to handpick correspondences. The proposed method introduces an attention-driven meta-network to model the relative affinities among features, and makes use of these inferred relations to regulate the intensity of distillation across all candidate feature pairs. Consequently, this automated approach discovers effective feature links more rapidly than prior work and achieves improved accuracy in both model reduction and transfer learning applications. Additional qualitative evidence and ablation experiments further elucidate the advantages offered by our method for the distillation process. Source code can be found at github.com/clovaai/attention-feature-distillation.

author: Bernard
title: Dynamic Weighting of Multiple Teachers via Reinforcement for Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Pre-trained deep models used for natural language processing frequently suffer from slow inference and high GPU resource consumption, which limit their deployment in real-world scenarios. Knowledge distillation, widely adopted for compressing models, enables a compact student model to acquire knowledge from one or more expansive teacher models. Prevailing approaches to distillation that employ several teachers generally keep a fixed importance weight for each teacher throughout training, and commonly distribute weights evenly among all teachers. In this study, we find that varying the learning emphasis across teacher models, in accordance with differences in both individual training samples and student model abilities, can enhance the distilled student's performance. To address this, we introduce a reinforced framework that adaptively determines the contribution of each teacher model for every training example with the goal of optimizing the student model. Comprehensive experiments across diverse NLP benchmarks demonstrate the practicality and superiority of the proposed method.

author: Rogers
title: A Confidence-Weighted Approach to Knowledge Distillation with Multiple Teachers
abstract: Knowledge distillation was first proposed as a method for training student models by drawing extra guidance from a single teacher model. In pursuit of superior student outcomes, later approaches have sought to leverage information from multiple teacher models. Prior work in this direction primarily aggregates knowledge from several sources through averaging teacher outputs or employing other methods that do not use labels, approaches which can potentially confuse the student if some teacher predictions lack quality. Addressing this concern, the proposed method introduces a confidence-based framework for multi-teacher distillation. This approach dynamically determines how much to trust each teacher's prediction for each training sample by using ground-truth labels; predictions by teachers that are more similar to the one-hot labels are given greater influence. Additionally, the method involves the use of intermediate layer information to make the transfer of knowledge more robust. Comprehensive experimental evaluations demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves superior and consistent performance compared to all evaluated state-of-the-art approaches over a range of student and teacher architecture pairings.

author: Davis
title: Adversarial Training-Based Online Distillation Incorporating Feature Map Distributions
abstract: Feature maps provide extensive details relating to spatial structure and pixel intensity in images. While earlier work on online knowledge distillation has been limited to transferring class probability information, we introduce a new online distillation strategy that conveys both class probability and feature map representations by utilizing adversarial training. Our approach simultaneously updates several networks by assigning each network a dedicated discriminator tasked with differentiating between its own feature maps and those produced by other networks—labeling its own as fake and others as real. Each network is optimized to deceive its discriminator, thereby learning the statistical distribution of feature maps from others. Comparative experiments reveal that this approach outperforms standard direct alignment strategies such as L1 loss for online distillation. Furthermore, we detail a new cyclic training strategy that extends our method to seamlessly distill knowledge among more than two simultaneous networks. Evaluation across diverse network architectures and classification benchmarks demonstrates notable performance enhancements, particularly when training a small and a large network in tandem.

author: Abbott
title: Adversarially-Guided Knowledge Distillation to Reduce the Size of Deep Graph Neural Networks
abstract: While graph neural networks with deep architectures are recognized for their capacity to capture patterns in graph-structured data, their considerable depth can be problematic when efficient deployment and fast iteration are needed on resource-constrained devices. The compression of such extensive GNNs frequently makes use of a teacher-student knowledge distillation framework; in this approach, a distance metric gauges the difference between the outputs of the teacher and student. Selecting a universal distance measure can be suboptimal across diverse graph types, and identifying the most effective formulation for this comparison remains challenging. To address these limitations, we introduce a different adversarial knowledge distillation strategy for graph models, relying on training both a generator and a discriminator adversarially to dynamically recognize and reduce divergence between teacher and student. The approach capitalizes on the observation that effective GNNs depend heavily on the preservation of both inter-class and inter-node relationships, and therefore, we employ a learnable discriminator to assess the transfer of such knowledge at both the node and class levels. The discriminator attempts to separate information originating from the teacher from that derived by the student, while the student GNN adopts the role of generator with the objective of deceiving the discriminator. As far as we are aware, this is the initial use of adversarial training to support knowledge distillation in the context of graph-based models. Evaluation on standard benchmarks for graph-level and node-level classification reveals that the proposed approach substantially boosts the capabilities of student models, supporting the conclusion that precise knowledge transfer from large teacher GNNs to smaller student models is achievable with this method.

author: Munoz
title: Data-Free Distillation for Deep Network Compression
abstract: When transferring knowledge from a high-capacity Teacher network to a compact Student model, knowledge distillation typically relies on either the original training dataset or information derived from it. Yet, direct use of such data can be impractical due to factors like dataset size or limitations imposed by confidentiality or risk, such as with sensitive biometric or clinical datasets. In this work, we introduce an approach that enables Student model training in the absence of both training data and derived meta-data. Our method creates synthetic Data Impressions by harnessing representations within the pretrained Teacher, which are then used in place of the original dataset during the distillation process to communicate the Teacher’s learned information to the Student. This procedure, which does not require any access to the Teacher’s training inputs, shows that the distilled Student achieves generalization performance on par with Students trained using the real data, as evidenced by experiments carried out on established benchmarking tasks.

author: Roman
title: Feature Distillation Methods to Enhance Fairness in Visual Recognition
abstract: Ensuring fairness is increasingly important in the context of computer vision, particularly for systems that make decisions affecting humans. Despite its significance, designing models that yield outcome distributions unaffected by group membership remains a challenging, open issue. This study introduces a feature distillation framework for visual recognition aimed at reducing algorithmic bias, referred to as the proposed method, which employs maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) as its foundation. Although distillation has been predominantly applied for boosting classification performance, prior literature has, to our knowledge, not explicitly leveraged distillation to enhance fairness. Additionally, we offer a theoretical analysis supporting both the fairness and knowledge transfer effects achieved by our strategy. Through comprehensive experiments, we demonstrate that the proposed method effectively lessens bias toward minority groups with no deterioration in performance, validated on both artificial and real-world facial image benchmarks.

author: Blair
title: A Comprehensive Analysis of Policy Distillation Approaches
abstract: In Deep Reinforcement Learning, transferring knowledge between policies serves as a fundamental process. This approach, termed distillation, has effectively accelerated agent optimisation and improved their ability to handle more challenging environments. Although distillation is prevalent and conceptually clear, its practical implementations vary considerably, and seemingly minor differences can significantly affect both the learning objectives and ultimate performance. This study undertakes a thorough examination of policy distillation methods, providing both theoretical justification and empirical validation for the comparison of their underlying motivations and advantages. Our findings identify three principal distillation strategies, each suitable for particular task requirements. Notably, the proposed variant based on expected entropy regularisation demonstrates enhanced speed of learning across various settings, while maintaining guarantees on convergence.

author: Herrera
title: Enhancing Object Detector Compression Through Localized Feature Response Alignment
abstract: Contemporary convolutional neural network recognition models achieve high accuracy but often require substantial computational resources, limiting their applicability on devices with restricted hardware capabilities. Knowledge distillation presents an effective overarching strategy, allowing a smaller student model to enhance its generalization by emulating the output of a more complex teacher model. While most prior approaches have concentrated on classification tasks, their extension to more intricate problems such as object detection has received less attention. We observe that directly applying conventional knowledge distillation techniques to detection architectures yields only marginal improvements. To better facilitate knowledge transfer in object detection frameworks, the proposed method introduces a mechanism that leverages fine-grained feature imitation, focusing on the spatial variability of feature activations. Recognizing that object detectors prioritize regions surrounding object locations, we hypothesize that differences in feature responses at anchor positions near objects are especially informative regarding the teacher model’s generalization. The method involves identifying these critical anchor locations and directing the student model to closely match the teacher’s feature responses at these points, resulting in improved performance. This intuition is first examined using a lightweight, custom-built toy detector embodying fundamental characteristics of current anchor-based detection systems, evaluated on the KITTI benchmark. Here, the proposed approach achieves up to a 15% increase in mAP relative to a baseline student without feature imitation. Further, comprehensive comparisons using the Faster R-CNN architecture on the Pascal VOC and COCO datasets demonstrate that the method reduces student-teacher performance gaps by as much as 74%. The codebase is accessible at https://github.com/twangnh/Distilling-Object-Detectors

author: Dudley
title: Utilizing Attention-Based Knowledge Distillation for Enhanced Reading Comprehension Models
abstract: While machine reading comprehension models have recently experienced notable progress, such improvements are typically achieved through combining multiple models in ensemble frameworks. In addition, these models remain susceptible to adversarial manipulations. The present work addresses these issues by employing knowledge distillation to convey the ensemble's information to a lone model. Initial findings indicate that applying standard knowledge distillation techniques to the task of identifying answer spans improves the effectiveness of reading comprehension systems. Furthermore, this study introduces two new strategies: these both apply a penalty to predictions associated with ambiguous answer choices and incorporate training signals based on alignment data distilled from the ensemble. Empirical results reveal that the top-performing student model maintains a minimal performance decrease of 0.4% in F1 score on the SQuAD test relative to its ensemble teacher, while achieving a twelvefold increase in inference speed. The student model also surpasses its teacher when evaluated on adversarial SQuAD versions as well as the NarrativeQA assessment.

author: Gray
title: A Progressive Module Replacement Strategy for BERT Model Compression
abstract: This work introduces an alternative technique for compressing BERT that employs incremental substitution of model modules. The method begins by partitioning BERT into multiple modules and designing smaller versions for each segment. During training, the process involves stochastic replacement of original modules with their compact counterparts, training these new modules to emulate the functional output of the originals. The likelihood of substitution is gradually increased as training proceeds. This process fosters substantial interaction between the full-size and reduced models. Unlike established BERT compression strategies based on knowledge distillation, this proposed method does not require supplementary loss functions. Evaluations on the GLUE benchmark demonstrate that the method achieves superior performance in comparison to existing knowledge distillation approaches, offering a novel viewpoint on model compression.

author: Arnold
title: Evaluating the Practical Effectiveness of Knowledge Distillation
abstract: A widely used approach in neural network training involves guiding a compact student network to approximate the behavior of a more complex teacher model—often a network ensemble—via knowledge distillation. Our findings indicate that although this process can enhance the ability of the student to generalize, the outcome does not typically align with prevailing assumptions: considerable differences frequently persist in the output distributions between student and teacher models, including in situations where the student network is theoretically capable of imitating the teacher entirely. We pinpoint challenges related to optimization as a significant factor in preventing the student from reaching equivalence with the teacher. Furthermore, we demonstrate that specifics of the dataset employed in the distillation process affect the extent to which the student replicates the teacher, and, counterintuitively, achieving a closer match to the teacher’s outputs does not necessarily result in improved generalization for the student.

author: Calderon
title: Generalizing Deep Models for Vehicle Routing through Cross-Distribution Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Typical neural approaches to vehicle routing problems are trained and evaluated within distributions of instances that match (specifically, uniform). Addressing the issue of limited transfer to alternative distributions, this work introduces knowledge distillation to the domain. The proposed method applies a multi-teacher knowledge distillation approach spanning several representative distributions in order to train a compact student network with broad applicability. This framework integrates an adaptive mechanism, enabling the student to focus on more challenging distributions for improved acquisition of complex knowledge. Experiments demonstrate that, in comparison to established neural baselines, the proposed method matches or exceeds performance on both novel in-distribution and out-of-distribution inputs, with test cases generated at random and drawn from standard datasets such as TSPLIB and CVRPLIB. Furthermore, the approach is designed to be architecture-agnostic and offers reduced inference demands.

author: Montgomery
title: Dynamic Graph-Based Approach for 3D Object Detection in Point Clouds
abstract: Identifying objects in three-dimensional data typically entails intricate procedures for both training and evaluation, along with considerable reliance on dataset-specific expertise. Taking motivation from 2D object detectors that do not utilize non-maximum suppression, we introduce a point cloud-based 3D object detection framework. This technique formulates object prediction as information exchange across dynamically constructed graphs, thereby extending DGCNN to generating collections of object outputs. Our formulation obviates the requirement for steps such as merging object confidences or applying non-maximum suppression during inference. In addition, to better handle detection in settings with few points, we present a set-to-set distillation method specifically adapted for 3D object detection. This method ensures permutation-invariant matching of teacher and student outputs, thereby making knowledge transfer between models for the 3D detection scenario more straightforward. The proposed strategy realizes state-of-the-art outcomes on benchmarks for autonomous vehicle applications. Comprehensive examination of both the detection strategy and the distillation approach is also included.

author: Hensley
title: Enhancing Low-Precision Network Performance through Application of Knowledge Distillation Methods
abstract: Recent advancements in deep learning have enabled networks to attain leading accuracy on vision tasks such as classification and detection. Nevertheless, such models often possess substantial size and parameter counts, making deployment on inference platforms with limited resources problematic due to heavy computational and storage demands. Knowledge distillation and reduced-precision arithmetic are established strategies to decrease both computational load and model size in deployment contexts. This study examines the synergy between these approaches, demonstrating that leveraging knowledge distillation can markedly boost the accuracy of networks trained with low-precision weights. Through the proposed method, state-of-the-art results are obtained on variants of the ResNet architecture employing ternary and 4-bit numerical formats on the ImageNet benchmark. We detail three procedures through which knowledge distillation can be utilized at different phases of the training and deployment process.

author: Ray
title: Transmitting Inductive Bias Effects via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Inductive biases play a pivotal role in settings where data availability or computational capacity is constrained, or when there is a mismatch between training and testing distributions. Yet, identifying, constructing, and modifying these biases is often complex. This work investigates how knowledge distillation can serve as a mechanism to pass on the influence of inductive biases between models. We evaluate this process in contexts where such biases are essential, focusing on pairs of modeling approaches with contrasting inductive biases such as LSTMs versus Transformers, and CNNs versus MLPs. Our analysis examines both the solutions reached by these models and the manner, as well as the degree, to which knowledge distillation transfers inductive bias impacts to distilled models, considering not just metrics of performance, but also multiple dimensions of the resultant solutions.

author: Bush
title: Knowledge Distillation from Weakly-Supervised Detection for Multi-Label Image Classification
abstract: Tackling multi-label image classification remains central and nontrivial in achieving comprehensive visual interpretation. Prior works have shown that incorporating region-based information, such as features extracted from RoIs, enhances multi-label classification outcomes. However, these techniques typically depend on detailed manual object annotations, like bounding boxes and individual object labels, which are labor-intensive to collect. This study introduces a deep learning framework that elevates multi-label classification outcomes through knowledge distillation from a weakly-supervised detection model that relies solely on image-level labels, with no need for bounding box annotations. The approach involves two main components: (1) training a weakly-supervised detection network using image-level supervision, and (2) embedding this detection model's guidance into an end-to-end multi-label classification architecture using a distillation process. Here, the detection model serves in the teacher role, while the classification network is the student; the student is supervised using both the overall image class predictions and the visual feature outputs for region proposals provided by the teacher. This cross-task distillation process leads to notable improvement in classification accuracy, while ensuring efficiency since the detection (teacher) model is not required during inference. Comprehensive evaluations on the MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing leading techniques in both accuracy and computational efficiency.

author: Williams
title: Relational Knowledge Distillation for Efficient Link Prediction Without Edge Inputs
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are highly successful in link prediction tasks, yet their reliance on extensive neighborhood information induces considerable inference delays, posing challenges for real-world use. Multilayer Perceptrons (MLPs), recognized for their computational efficiency, generally underperform in this context owing to their insufficient access to relational structure. This study investigates several straightforward knowledge distillation (KD) strategies for link prediction, such as aligning the output logits or node embeddings between GNN teachers and MLP students. Finding that these direct KD approaches exhibit subpar effectiveness for link prediction, we introduce a relational KD technique that transfers relational information to an MLP for link prediction without utilizing explicit edge connectivity. Unlike conventional KD which matches the predicted logits or embeddings of individual links or nodes, our approach imparts neighborhood-based relational context centered around each anchor node to the student MLP. We devise both rank-oriented and distribution-oriented alignment mechanisms, designed to be mutually reinforcing. Through comprehensive empirical evaluation, our method markedly improves MLP link prediction performance and secures higher accuracy than the original GNN teachers on seven of eight evaluation datasets. In addition, the proposed approach delivers a 70.68-fold reduction in inference time for link prediction compared to GNN architectures on the large-scale OGB benchmark.

author: Perez
title: Domain Adaptation Utilizing Predictions from Black-Box Models in Both Single and Multiple Source Scenarios
abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) transfers information from labeled source datasets to a target dataset without labels, reducing the effort required for manual annotation. Most earlier approaches depend on direct access to original source data and use strategies based on those data for aligning source and target distributions. However, such reliance may lead to privacy issues for source data holders. Recent alternatives instead employ fully transparent (white-box) source models, but these methods could inadvertently expose original data when using generative adversarial learning techniques. This work addresses a more constrained and realistic UDA situation, where the adaptation process is limited to the use of black-box source models, meaning only the network outputs are observable within the target domain. To handle this challenge, this paper introduces a two-phase adaptation approach: the proposed method initially extracts knowledge from the outputs of the source model and transfers it to a target-specific model, and then further adapts this initial model to better adjust to the target dataset. This solution is designed to account for the structure of the target data and does not require that model architectures match between source and target, making adaptation possible even with limited computational resources. Extensive evaluation across three types of UDA tasks—single-source, multiple-source, and partial-set—demonstrates that the proposed method matches or surpasses leading techniques that use source data directly. Repository for the code is accessible at https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/.

author: Roberts
title: Enhancing Deep Neural Network Explainability via Transferring Knowledge to Decision Trees
abstract: Deep Neural Networks have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across numerous domains including computer vision, language modeling, and speech recognition. Yet, strong predictive performance is increasingly insufficient for many real-world applications, especially in settings that require transparency for ethical or safety-critical reasons. The intricate modeling of Deep Neural Networks presents challenges in interpreting model outputs, restraining their adoption in sensitive contexts. To address this, the proposed method leverages Knowledge Distillation to transfer the learned representations from Deep Neural Networks into decision trees, thereby aiming to balance predictive accuracy with interpretability. This approach is cast as a multi-output regression task, and empirical results reveal that the student models surpass standard decision trees in accuracy by approximately 1% to 5% for equivalent tree depths. All experiments are conducted on large-scale datasets using the TensorFlow framework to ensure scalability. As far as is known, this study represents the first effort to employ distillation from Deep Neural Networks into standard decision trees for multi-class problems.

author: Miller
title: Examining the Effect of Distillation on BERT-Based Ranking Models
abstract: Extensive advancements in information retrieval ranking have resulted from the use of deep language architectures like BERT, which are trained on expansive text datasets. These models capture intricate relationships between queries and passages due to the knowledge they acquire. Nevertheless, practical deployment often faces obstacles due to their substantial inference computational requirements. This work investigates the transfer of BERT's search capabilities to a compact ranking model using distillation. Our findings show that adopting an appropriate distillation strategy is essential; with this approach, we achieve as much as a 9-fold improvement in inference speed while maintaining leading edge performance.

author: Hall
title: Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer for Federated Learning with Diverse and Resource-Limited On-Device Models
abstract: Federated learning offers a framework for multiple devices to cooperatively construct a common prediction model while retaining data locally. Prevailing approaches typically necessitate that each device conducts training with models of uniform architecture and scale, which can be problematic for devices with limited computational capacity. In response to the diversity and constraints of contemporary devices, this work introduces a federated learning approach in which model structures may vary across devices; knowledge is exchanged via zero-shot distillation, referred to here as the proposed method. In detail, devices are empowered to select their own model configurations based on their individual resource limitations. To support the transfer of knowledge among these differing on-device models, a distillation method operating in a zero-shot manner is devised, eliminating the need for either public data or pre-trained data synthesis tools, unlike several earlier methods. This distillation, which requires significant computational power, is offloaded to the central server, thereby permitting devices with restricted resources to participate; the server collaboratively trains a generator using an adversarial strategy and the ensemble of received device models. Afterwards, consolidated knowledge is provided back to the devices as their own model parameter updates, enabling seamless integration. Comprehensive experiments confirm that the proposed approach is both effective and robust across settings involving agnostic device-side knowledge, varying device model architectures, and further challenging circumstances such as non-uniform data distributions and variable device participation.

author: Garcia
title: Knowledge Distillation for Reducing Visual-Linguistic Model Size
abstract: While extensive advancements have been made in pre-training for representations that combine vision and language, there is limited focus on developing compact models for these tasks. This work investigates the application of knowledge distillation to condense a transformer-driven, large-scale visual-linguistic model into a more compact one. A central difficulty stems from the discrepancy between regional visual tokens generated by the Teacher’s and Student’s detectors, causing a mismatch in intermediate features and transformer attention patterns. To mitigate this, the Teacher is retrained and modified: although the region proposals are sourced from the Student’s detector, the feature extraction still uses the Teacher’s object detector. By synchronizing the inputs to both networks, the modified Teacher can effectively distill knowledge through intermediary feature spaces. Our methodology employs mean square error loss to transfer attention maps from the Teacher’s transformer blocks, and introduces a token-level noise contrastive loss that matches the Student’s hidden representations to those of the Teacher, in contrast to negative samples aggregated in a queue. Experiments demonstrate that this distillation technique yields notable performance boosts for smaller visual-linguistic models in both image captioning and visual question answering benchmarks. Specifically, on COCO image captioning, a CIDEr score of 120.8 is achieved, surpassing the non-distilled model by 5.1, while on VQA 2.0, the accuracy reaches 69.8, representing a 0.8 improvement over the baseline. Comprehensive empirical analysis and ablation studies confirm the benefit of the proposed distillation approach during both pre-training and fine-tuning.

author: Ramirez
title: Teacher-Free Distillation via Incremental Adjustment of Prediction Targets
abstract: A broad array of regularization strategies, including constraints on function classes, stochastic perturbations during optimization, and data manipulation techniques, have notably boosted the generalization of deep neural networks. This paper introduces a straightforward regularization approach, referred to here as the proposed method, which incrementally distills knowledge from the network itself to gradually transform rigid one-hot labels into softer targets throughout learning. This process aligns conceptually with knowledge distillation, where a single model sequentially assumes the roles of both student and teacher. Concretely, the method adapts targets on the fly by merging actual labels with the model’s previous output probabilities. It is demonstrated that this approach implicitly conducts hard example mining by scaling the loss gradients in accordance with the classification challenge posed by each instance. The proposed method is suitable for any supervised task with deterministic targets and is compatible with other regularization techniques, offering additional generalization gains. Moreover, empirical evidence indicates not only an increase in predictive accuracy but also improved confidence calibration and better ordinal prediction. Comprehensive experiments spanning image classification, object detection, and machine translation confirm that this method reliably enhances leading baseline results. Implementation resources can be found at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

author: Reid
title: Reducing Memory in Neural Networks through Distillation with Lightweight Convolutions
abstract: Deploying current neural network models in environments constrained by limited memory remains a challenge, as strategies for decreasing memory requirements are not yet well established and the associated trade-offs are inadequately understood. This work introduces a structural distillation approach for decreasing memory use, where the student model is derived from the teacher network via a straightforward modification, allowing retention of both the architecture's structure and its hyperparameters without needing to redesign them. By leveraging attention transfer, we present Pareto analyses—both in graphical and tabular form—of distillation applied to residual networks on four standard benchmark datasets, illustrating the balance between memory consumption and predictive accuracy. Our results demonstrate that large reductions in memory use can be achieved with minimal accuracy degradation, and further, that performing distillation yields student networks with higher accuracy compared to models of the same architecture trained from scratch on the data.

author: Diaz
title: Two-phase Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation Approach for Compressing Models in Web-based Question Answering Applications
abstract: Recent advances in deep pre-trained and fine-tuned models, including those like BERT and OpenAI GPT, have achieved state-of-the-art performance in question answering settings. Nonetheless, the extensive number of parameters in these models causes significant delays in inference, hindering their deployment in practice-oriented business environments. Existing compression techniques frequently incur a deterioration in model quality due to loss of information throughout the compression process, resulting in models that lag behind their original counterparts. To address this, the proposed method introduces a two-phase approach using multi-teacher knowledge distillation specifically designed for web-based question answering systems. The first phase involves constructing a universal question answering distillation objective for the pre-training of the student model. This is followed by an additional fine-tuning step, utilizing knowledge from multiple teachers through distillation across several downstream benchmarks (such as Web Question Answering, MNLI, SNLI, and RTE tasks from the GLUE suite), thereby mitigating the overfitting tendencies of single teacher models and imparting broader knowledge frameworks to the student architecture. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that the proposed method consistently surpasses baseline compression schemes and in some cases reaches performance levels on par with the original teacher models, while also delivering notable improvements in inference efficiency.

author: Wood
title: A Statistical Examination of Effective Data Augmentation in Knowledge Distillation
abstract: The process of knowledge distillation (KD) involves training neural networks by leveraging a teacher model to supervise a student model. Much prior research has concentrated on modeling improvements at the output level, such as proposing novel KD loss functions, but investigation into input-level factors has been limited. In particular, the interaction between knowledge distillation and data augmentation (DA) is not yet thoroughly understood. This study explores questions including why certain DA techniques, such as CutMix, appear to outperform alternatives within the context of KD, and seeks to define what characterizes an effective DA approach for distillation. Our statistical analysis indicates that DA methods that decrease the covariance between teacher and student cross-entropy provide advantages. We introduce a quantitative measure—the standard deviation of the teacher's mean probability (T. stddev)—and validate its relevance through experiments. Alongside theoretical analysis, we propose a supplementary DA method based on entropy-driven data mixing intended to improve upon CutMix, referred to here as the proposed method. Extensive experimentation confirms our hypotheses and shows that notable improvements in student performance during KD can be achieved by adopting more suitable DA strategies.

author: Clark
title: A Knowledge Distillation Approach for High-Resolution Universal Style Transfer with Encoder-Decoder Models
abstract: Universal style transfer commonly relies on detailed features extracted by convolutional neural networks such as VGG-19, which have been pre-trained on extensive image datasets. While this technique brings strong performance, processing images at extremely high resolutions is restricted by the considerable memory requirements of the standard architectures. Here, we introduce a novel approach based on knowledge distillation, specifically designed for neural style transfer frameworks employing encoder-decoder configurations, with the goal of minimizing the number of convolutional filters. The approach is motivated by observing that encoder and decoder components form a unique interplay, representing supplementary knowledge for style transfer purposes. To address discrepancies in feature dimensionality that arise during our distillation process, we incorporate a linear embedding loss, encouraging the student model to approximate a linear transformation of the teacher network’s features. Detailed experimental studies demonstrate that the proposed method remains effective for several universal style transfer techniques, including WCT and AdaIN, achieving up to a 15.5-fold reduction in model size. Notably, with compressed models based on WCT, our strategy enables universal style transfer on images exceeding 40 megapixels using a 12GB GPU for the first time. Additional tests with optimization-based stylization strategies confirm the adaptability of our approach across different stylization methods. Code and pretrained models are publicly accessible at https://github.com/mingsun-tse/collaborative-distillation.

author: Adams
title: Examining Deep Learning Practices: The Roles of Restarts, Warmup, and Knowledge Distillation in Model Training
abstract: Deep learning architectures frequently achieve faster convergence and improved outcomes as a result of practical strategies such as learning rate adjustments, application of knowledge distillation, use of skip connections, and inclusion of normalization layers. Clarifying how these commonly used techniques function, despite a lack of formal theoretical explanation, requires systematic experiments designed to illuminate the intricacies of training and model landscape exploration. While current empirical studies typically utilize linear interpolation and dimensionality reduction visual tools, these methodologies have their shortcomings. This work presents an alternative approach, making use of contemporary analytic techniques focused on loss landscape characterization and feature representation analysis—specifically, mode connectivity and canonical correlation analysis (CCA). The study formulates hypotheses about the mechanisms underlying these practical training strategies' effectiveness. Centered on knowledge distillation, cosine learning rate restarts, and warmup methods, our investigation leverages both mode connectivity and CCA. Our results indicate: (a) popular explanations for the effectiveness of cosine learning rate schedules lack empirical support in our experimental context; (b) learning rate warmup appears primarily to reduce training instability in the network’s deeper layers; and (c) most of the implicit information communicated by the teacher through distillation is directed towards the lower layers of the student network.

author: Zuniga
title: Scaling distributed neural network optimization with concurrent distillation
abstract: Model enhancements such as ensembling and distillation typically provide improvements in model performance across various architectures, yet ensembling introduces significant inference overhead, and distillation often increases training system complexity, complicating adoption in production environments. This study investigates a straightforward distillation approach that avoids elaborate multi-phase processes and does not introduce a multitude of new hyperparameters. We firstly demonstrate that concurrent ("online") distillation leverages additional parallel computational resources to allow fitting of massive datasets at approximately double the previous speed. Notably, this acceleration persists beyond the stage where extra parallelism fails to further expedite either synchronous or asynchronous SGD. In our method, two separate neural networks, each processing a distinct partition of the data, are encouraged to align their output distributions, with each model nudged toward the outcomes its peer would predict. These peer predictions may be delivered from delayed model checkpoints, requiring infrequent parameter sharing. Secondly, we show that this distillation strategy greatly increases the reproducibility of model predictions at minimal additional expense. These findings are substantiated by empirical results on the Criteo Display Ad Challenge, ImageNet, and the largest neural language modeling dataset used to date, comprising $6	imes 10^{11}$ tokens from Common Crawl web data.

author: Wong
title: Utilizing Knowledge Distillation with Regularization for Enhanced Domain Generalization
abstract: Convolutional neural networks have become standard across various applications, yet their performance often decreases when faced with insufficient or non-representative datasets, limiting their broader usage. This work introduces a straightforward and broadly applicable training approach based on knowledge distillation, supplemented by a novel gradient-based regularizer, to address this issue. The approach, referred to here as the proposed method, leverages both the comprehensive information found in teacher network outputs (i.e., dark knowledge) and the gradient regularization term to facilitate the mapping process during training, resulting in improved generalization. Comprehensive empirical evaluation demonstrates that this framework yields considerable gains in generalization for deep neural networks across diverse tasks, such as image classification, segmentation, and reinforcement learning, when benchmarked against leading domain generalization methods. Additionally, two quantitative measures are employed to further examine and illustrate how the proposed method contributes to enhancing the generalization of deep neural network models.

author: Lynch
title: Analyzing the Connection Between Knowledge Distillation and Label Smoothing Regularization
abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) involves transferring information from a large teacher model to a more compact student model. The effectiveness of KD is commonly ascribed to the teacher providing insight into inter-class relationships, and it is thus standard practice to use only high-performing teachers to instruct weaker students. In contrast, our experimental findings reveal: (1) not only can students benefit from teachers, but reversing the KD direction allows the student to considerably benefit the teacher as well; (2) even teachers with much poorer training performance than the student can still lead to substantial student improvements. We account for these findings by developing a theoretical framework that connects KD to label smoothing regularization. Specifically, we establish that: (1) KD can be viewed as a specialized instance of label smoothing that is learned, and (2) employing label smoothing regularization is akin to introducing an implicit teacher within KD. These insights suggest that attributing KD's effectiveness solely to the teacher's inter-class similarity cues overlooks the equally (or more) significant role played by the regularizing impact of using soft targets. Building on this perspective, we introduce a Teacher-free Knowledge Distillation (Tf-KD) approach, which enables a student model to leverage either its own predictions or a distribution crafted via manual regularization. Tf-KD matches the performance achieved with conventional KD using a strong teacher, providing a practical option when such teachers are not available. This method is readily applicable during the training of deep neural networks, and without increasing computational demands, Tf-KD delivers up to a 0.65% gain on ImageNet compared to robust baselines, outperforming standard label smoothing regularization.

author: Jackson
title: Mutual Contrastive Learning for Teacher-Free Online Knowledge Distillation in Visual Recognition
abstract: In teacher-free online Knowledge Distillation settings, multiple student models are jointly optimized to exchange knowledge with each other during training. Prior work in this area generally emphasizes class probability outputs, frequently overlooking the significance of sharing feature representations. In this study, we introduce a framework based on Mutual Contrastive Learning for online knowledge transfer. Our method enables networks to interact by sharing and aligning contrastive distributions online across the ensemble. By encouraging the exchange of embedding information between networks, our framework maximizes a lower bound on mutual information between their representations. As a result, participating models are able to acquire new contrastive knowledge from their peers, which enhances the learned feature representations and boosts performance on visual recognition benchmarks. In addition to targeting the last layer, the proposed framework is extended to intermediate representations, utilizing an adaptively-learned mechanism for selecting which layers to match, optimized through meta-learning techniques. Experimental evaluation on visual recognition tasks, including image classification and transfer learning, reveals that applying this layerwise Mutual Contrastive Learning leads to consistent improvements relative to existing state-of-the-art techniques for online Knowledge Distillation. These results indicate that the proposed mechanism fosters the creation of superior feature representations. The implementation used in this work is available at https://github.com/winycg/L-MCL.

author: Daniel
title: Adversarial Knowledge Distillation Without Dataset Access
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is widely recognized as a leading technique for compressing models and migrating knowledge, but current approaches overwhelmingly depend on access to large-scale authentic or synthetic datasets, a condition not often satisfied in practice. Addressing this limitation, we put forward a new adversarial strategy for distillation that constructs an efficient student model entirely without using real-world samples. Central to our method is a formal metric that captures the divergence between the student and teacher, for which we derive an upper bound that is amenable to optimization. Our framework assigns both the teacher and student to function collaboratively as a discriminator that seeks to minimize their divergence, while a generator adversarially creates "challenging samples" to exacerbate it. Through broad experimentation, we show that the described approach, which does not require any data, performs on par with standard data-dependent techniques. Notably, our technique is readily applicable to complex tasks like semantic segmentation, achieving results that match or surpass existing state-of-the-art. Source code and trained weights can be found at https://github.com/VainF/Data-Free-Adversarial-Distillation.

author: Martin
title: Transferring BERT Knowledge to Sequence-to-Sequence Models for Speech Recognition
abstract: Sequence-to-sequence models with attention mechanisms have yielded strong outcomes in automatic speech recognition tasks. Nevertheless, these models generate output in a left-to-right manner, which restricts their access to future context. To address this, we incorporate BERT as an auxiliary language model into sequence-to-sequence ASR via knowledge distillation.
