The proposed approach involves BERT producing probabilistic targets that supervise the training process of the ASR system. Additionally, input to BERT includes contextual information extending past the current utterance. Our experiments demonstrate that this strategy leads to marked enhancements over the standard sequence-to-sequence baseline on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ). The use of BERT for knowledge distillation achieves better results than employing a transformer language model restricted to left context. The benefit of utilizing extra-utterance context is also validated. Compared to other ways of incorporating language models, such as n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, our method attains higher accuracy without incurring additional inference time.

author: Gray
title: Enhancing Feature Distillation Through Multiple Projector Networks
abstract: Feature distillation within knowledge distillation research has largely prioritized loss function formulation and determining which network layers to distill, yet the influence of the feature projector connecting teacher and student has not been thoroughly investigated. This study initially explores the role of the projector using empirical data before introducing a novel feature distillation technique that leverages an ensemble of projectors to achieve better student model performance. We find that incorporating a projector is advantageous for the student model even in cases where the feature sizes are identical between student and teacher. When a student backbone is trained without a projector, it effectively faces a multi-task learning scenario: extracting features that support classification and simultaneously matching representations with the teacher as required for distillation. Our hypothesis, which our experiments support, is that omitting the projector causes the student to overfit to the teacher's feature outputs, despite differences in their initialization and network structure. This overfitting compromises the suitability of the resulting feature representations for classification. Introducing a projector, however, separates these competing learning goals, allowing the student to concentrate on effective feature extraction for classification while still aligning with teacher features through the projector path. Building on the demonstrated utility of projectors in this context, we propose combining several projectors in an ensemble to further refine student feature learning. We validate the approach with experiments across diverse datasets and multiple teacher-student configuration pairs, showcasing its effectiveness.

author: Mayo
title: Analyzing the Bias and Variance Implications of Soft Label-Based Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Utilizing knowledge distillation, a well-established strategy, involves employing one or more pretrained networks—collectively referred to as the teacher—to inform the learning process of a student network. In this context, the teacher's output probabilities, known as soft labels, are adopted to supervise student model training. Prior research yuan2020revisiting, muller2019does has shown that incorporating soft labels into training can serve as a significant regularization method for the student. Although regularization in statistical learning typically aims to control variance, the precise influence on bias and variance when training with soft labels warrants further examination. This work focuses on exploring the bias-variance interplay introduced by applying soft labels via distillation. Our analysis uncovers that the tradeoff between bias and variance is dependent on individual samples during the learning process. Additionally, experiments using a fixed distillation temperature suggest that overall distillation success is disadvantaged by the presence of a subset of training examples we identify as regularization samples—these tend to increase bias while simultaneously lowering variance. However, eliminating these regularization samples entirely is found to harm the performance of the student. Motivated by these findings, we introduce a newly designed scheme employing weighted soft labels to facilitate adaptive management of the sample-level bias-variance compromise. Empirical assessment on widely used benchmark datasets confirms the proposed method's improved effectiveness. Implementation resources are accessible at https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation.

author: Bowman
title: Compact Paralinguistic Speech Embedding Models via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Recent progress in self-supervised learning has significantly advanced speech representation techniques. Nonetheless, real-world deployment of leading embedding systems remains hindered by their substantial computational demands and restricted access. To overcome these limitations, this study introduces a suite of lightweight paralinguistic speech models that are publicly accessible and achieve performance close to state-of-the-art. Relying exclusively on knowledge distillation from public datasets, several model architectures were developed and systematically assessed with the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark. The largest version produced through distillation occupies less than 15% of the memory required by the teacher network (314MB versus 2.2GB), attains above 96% of the teacher's accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks, and was trained with only 6.5% of the original data. The most compact model uses 1% of the storage (22MB) while surpassing 90% of the teacher’s accuracy on 6 of 7 evaluated tasks. On the NOSS benchmark, all proposed models outperform the released Wav2Vec 2.0 model on 6 of 7 tasks, with the smallest model achieving superior results on both emotion recognition tasks at approximately 7% of Wav2Vec 2.0's size.

author: Hawkins
title: An Accelerated Distillation Approach for Vision Tasks
abstract: Knowledge Distillation has been proven beneficial in several computer vision applications, spanning from supervised learning tasks to unsupervised feature learning. The conventional distillation strategy, however, entails considerable computational expense because of repeated forward passes through large teacher models, which limits its practical efficiency. A recent approach proposes generating label maps for full images in advance, where cropped region labels are obtained via RoI alignment during training, thereby reducing the need for multiple teacher evaluations. Nevertheless, due to a reliance on teachers derived from standard multi-crop data augmentation, this method suffers from inconsistencies between regional and whole-image label maps, diminishing final accuracy. In this work, we introduce a rapid distillation technique that reconstructs the distillation training step and yields soft label targets through a multi-crop based procedure, yet eliminates post-processing requirements such as RoI alignment and softmax, enabling faster operation than the aforementioned method. With multi-crop sampling employed within each image during data handling, our approach can be even more computationally efficient than standard classification pipelines. Experimental results on ImageNet-1K demonstrate a 79.8% accuracy using ResNet-50, approximately 1.0% higher than the previous label-mapping method while maintaining improved training speed. Additionally, on unsupervised representation learning benchmarks, our method also excels in terms of efficiency.

author: Cohen
title: Attention-Guided Layer Combination for Knowledge Distillation in Neural Networks
abstract: Knowledge distillation is utilized as both a training approach and a model compression method, involving simultaneous training of a teacher and a student neural network. The teacher model acts as a reliable reference, while the student attempts to approximate the teacher’s predictive outputs. Lighter-weight student networks are generally chosen to facilitate compression while aiming to retain strong performance. Conventional distillation strategies focus solely on matching the final output distributions, but students can also gain from supervisory signals on internal representations. Consequently, we address distillation at intermediate network layers. Because there is typically no direct correspondence between the layers of the student and those of the teacher, standard approaches only transfer knowledge from selected teacher layers, omitting others—a limitation that may affect effectiveness. In response, we introduce a method based on attention mechanisms that merges information across teacher layers, weighting each by its relative importance, to create a composite representation for distillation into student layers. We apply this approach to compress a 12-layer BERT model into student models with 6, 4, and 2 layers, assessing their performance on the GLUE benchmark suite. Our experiments demonstrate that this attention-based technique yields superior performance compared to previous distillation methods.

author: Cameron
title: The Value of Pre-training for Compact Language Models: Reevaluating Baselines and Knowledge Transfer
abstract: Large-scale breakthroughs in language model representations have led to models that are both computationally intensive and reliant on substantial self-supervised pre-training with general-domain corpora. To address the resource demands associated with deploying such models for downstream applications, various strategies to compress pre-trained language representations have been put forward. Nevertheless, the straightforward strategy of applying pre-training directly to compact models, followed by task-specific fine-tuning, has generally not received sufficient attention. This study demonstrates that pre-training holds significant benefit even for reduced-size architectures; fine-tuning such pre-trained compact models can perform on par with more intricate approaches introduced recently. Building on these pre-trained compact networks, we apply standard knowledge distillation to enable compact student models to acquire task knowledge from large, fine-tuned teacher models. This procedure—referred to here simply as pre-trained distillation—offers notable additional gains while remaining simple and broadly applicable. Our comprehensive experimental evaluation investigates how pre-training and distillation interact, specifically considering the effects of model capacity and the characteristics of available unlabeled data for the given task. We uncover that combining pre-training and distillation can yield synergistic improvements, even when both techniques are employed sequentially on the identical dataset. As a resource for subsequent research, we will release 24 pre-trained compact BERT model variants to the community.

author: Parsons
title: Optimizing Dense Retrieval Distillation via Curriculum-Based Training
abstract: Prior studies have demonstrated that dense retrieval models become more effective when the ranking information from a pre-trained re-ranking model is distilled into them. This work introduces an approach that utilizes curriculum learning to regulate the complexity of the training samples generated by the re-ranking (teacher) model. The proposed method incrementally improves the dense retrieval (student) model by gradually presenting it with more challenging distillation instances. Specifically, training starts with broader preference pairs among documents as determined by the teacher’s output, and then transitions toward more detailed pairwise ranking constraints. A straightforward implementation of this curriculum learning strategy is employed to boost the performance of two state-of-the-art dense retrieval architectures. Results from evaluation on three established passage retrieval benchmarks highlight the advantages conferred by the proposed method.

author: Perez
title: Multi-Task Knowledge Distillation with Teacher Annealing for Natural Language Understanding Tasks
abstract: Training neural networks for multiple tasks simultaneously often results in models that do not reach the performance of those trained for individual tasks. To mitigate this issue, this work applies knowledge distillation, employing models trained on single tasks as teachers to guide a multi-task student model. Additionally, a new training strategy called teacher annealing is introduced; this approach progressively shifts the focus from distillation to direct supervision, allowing the multi-task network to eventually outperform its single-task teachers. Using BERT as the backbone, the method is applied to multi-task fine-tuning on the GLUE benchmark. Across experiments, the proposed approach yields consistent gains over both conventional single-task and multi-task learning procedures.

author: Stewart
title: Protecting Privacy in Compressing Neural Networks Using Knowledge Distillation
abstract: The escalating need for intelligent features in mobile apps necessitates running large-scale deep neural networks (DNNs) directly on mobile hardware. Nevertheless, DNNs' high accuracy generally stems from their significant model size and computational requirements, which far exceed the processing abilities of mobile devices. Furthermore, service providers must handle substantial quantities of user data, which frequently includes private information, for training advanced DNNs, introducing considerable privacy concerns if these sophisticated models are deployed on users' devices. To enable practical on-device deep learning while mitigating constraints related to both model complexity and privacy, we introduce a privacy-preserving compression approach referred to here as the proposed method. Utilizing the framework of knowledge distillation, our strategy combines hint learning, distillation learning, and self learning to construct a streamlined neural architecture with increased efficiency. Throughout the distillation process, the information transferred from the larger network is adaptively limited and deliberately perturbed to adhere to differential privacy guarantees. Additionally, we develop a specialized query sample selection strategy that reduces the number of interactions required, thus limiting the associated privacy cost. Extensive experimentation and Android phone deployment demonstrate that the proposed method compresses large models effectively while maintaining robust privacy protection. On the SVHN benchmark, as an illustration, when ensuring differential privacy at the $(9.83, 10^{-6})$ level, our approach achieves a 20-fold reduction in model size and a 19-fold increase in execution speed, while incurring only a 0.97% drop in accuracy.

author: Adams
title: Reassessing the Relationship Between Label Smoothing and Knowledge Distillation: Experimental Insights
abstract: In this study, we systematically investigate the notion that label smoothing may not align with knowledge distillation from an empirical standpoint. The discussion opens with an examination of the reasoning for this purported incompatibility: specifically, that label smoothing diminishes the relative informativeness found in the teacher's logits. We establish a new link demonstrating how label smoothing impacts the distributions among classes with semantic similarity or dissimilarity. To provide a quantitative assessment, we introduce a novel metric designed to evaluate the extent of information loss in the representations of individual samples. Subsequently, we explore potential limitations and partial accuracy of the incompatibility hypothesis through extensive empirical analysis, visualization, and experiments across various tasks, including image recognition, binary neural architectures, and neural machine translation. We conclude with an in-depth discussion of multiple scenarios in which the effectiveness of label smoothing might be compromised.

author: Clark
title: Enabling Model-Agnostic Federated Collaboration via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Can a universally applicable interface for federated learning be established, allowing independently organized data-holders (agents) to jointly train models without restrictions on architecture or dependence on accessible public datasets? Realizing such an interface calls for a model-agnostic strategy. Knowledge distillation naturally arises as a means to facilitate these solutions. In this work, we demonstrate that a range of straightforward knowledge distillation-based federated learning strategies result in unsatisfactory outcomes. To examine this issue, we introduce a new analytic approach, which we refer to as Federated Kernel ridge regression, that models both the diversity in agents' models and their underlying data. Our theoretical insights attribute the observed failures primarily to an inherent deficiency of knowledge distillation when faced with data heterogeneity. We substantiate our analysis by evaluating and constructing alternative knowledge distillation-based schemes. Their observed results in practical neural network federated learning scenarios, while still falling short, are consistent with the theoretical expectations developed in our analysis.

author: Hahn
title: A Generalized Object Detector Distillation Method Using Pearson Correlation Coefficient
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has proven effective for training smaller object detection models. Nevertheless, approaches for transferring knowledge across divergent detector architectures remain underexplored. This study observes that superior FPN-derived features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can provide benefit to the student model, even when architectures of their detection heads and label assignment strategies vary. Nevertheless, naive feature map alignment in detector distillation introduces two challenges: significant differences in feature magnitude may impose excessively tight demands on the student, and FPN layers or channels with larger feature values in the teacher can disproportionately steer the distillation loss’s gradients, thereby drowning out contributions from other features and adding noise to the learning process. To mitigate these concerns, this work distills student feature representations using Pearson Correlation Coefficient, thereby prioritizing inter-feature relationships over direct magnitude constraints. The proposed method demonstrates greater effectiveness than prior detection KD techniques for both homogeneous and heterogeneous teacher-student configurations, in addition to exhibiting faster convergence. Using a strong MaskRCNN-Swin model as teacher, RetinaNet and FCOS models based on ResNet-50 achieve mAP values of 41.5% and 43.9% on COCO2017, representing improvements of 4.1% and 4.8% over their respective baselines.

author: Walter
title: Distilling Knowledge Effectively from Teachers with Superior Performance
abstract: Most previous approaches to knowledge distillation have concentrated on scenarios involving standard teacher models and non-cutting-edge training techniques, rather than leveraging more powerful teachers trained with advanced methods. The approach introduced in this work addresses this gap by targeting the transfer of knowledge from a stronger teacher. Our experiments reveal that when the teacher outperforms the student by a large margin, their prediction outputs differ much more, leading to significant challenges for students trained using KL divergence to closely match the teacher’s logits; this difficulty reduces the effectiveness of traditional methods. To address this, we demonstrate that it is sufficient for the student to maintain the relational information present between its predictions and those of the teacher. Accordingly, we propose a loss function based on correlation to allow the student to explicitly learn the inter-class relationships inherent in the teacher’s output. Additionally, recognizing that each data instance exhibits varying semantic proximity to different classes, we further enhance the approach by applying the relational alignment at the intra-class level. This straightforward yet effective method has been validated through comprehensive experiments, showing robust improvement across diverse network architectures, model scales, and training regimes, and providing consistently competitive performance for image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation benchmarks. The implementation is publicly accessible at the provided URL: https://github.com/hunto/DIST_KD .

author: Edwards
title: Enhancing Privacy in Federated Learning via Aggregated Noisy Cross-Domain Knowledge Transfer
abstract: Federated Learning allows multiple distributed clients to construct a shared model without transferring local datasets to a centralized location. Current techniques in this area tend to rely on either synchronization of model weights or collaborative distillation across clients to mitigate non-iid data distributions. Nonetheless, these approaches encounter significant communication overhead and face privacy exposure risks. In this study, we introduce an approach for federated learning that achieves both privacy protection and communication efficiency by applying a one-time, offline knowledge distillation step utilizing unlabeled data drawn from diverse public sources. Our strategy gathers quantized and noise-added prediction outputs from locally finalized models into an ensemble, thereby strengthening privacy defenses while retaining model performance. Through comprehensive evaluation on both visual and textual classification benchmarks, our privacy-focused method demonstrates superiority over standard federated learning baselines, achieving higher accuracy and reduced communication demands.

author: Rios
title: Enhancing Topic Quality in Neural Models via Teacher-Student Training
abstract: Neural topic models enable extraction of understandable topics for analysis of extensive text corpora. In this work, we employ knowledge distillation to merge strengths from both probabilistic topic modeling algorithms and pretrained transformer architectures. The approach we introduce is modular and can be incorporated into any neural topic model for better topic representation. We validate its effectiveness by applying it to two structurally distinct models, achieving leading results in terms of topic coherence. Additionally, our flexible framework yields performance improvements not just in overall topic evaluation—a standard in the field—but also when directly comparing corresponding topics.

author: Foster
title: Utilizing Ensembled Teacher Models for Knowledge Distillation in Click-Through Rate Prediction
abstract: Deep learning methods have become prevalent in the task of click-through rate (CTR) prediction, leading to advances in predictive performance for various industrial scenarios. Most existing efforts concentrate on engineering increasingly sophisticated network designs to capture intricate relationships among features and account for evolving user patterns. Nevertheless, these intricate models may introduce latency during inference, limiting their practicality for latency-sensitive, real-time environments. This study addresses this concern by introducing a training paradigm centered on knowledge distillation (KD), a teacher-student paradigm that facilitates the transfer of learned representations from a teacher model to a student model. In this context, the KD procedure enables the student network, implemented as a standard deep neural network, to realize meaningful gains in prediction accuracy when compared with leading teacher models, while remaining relatively simple. Motivated by these outcomes, we examine training with multiple teacher models combined in an ensemble to further enhance student model efficacy. Furthermore, the proposed method integrates additional strategies intended to optimize the ensemble KD process for CTR prediction, specifically the application of teacher gating and distillation loss-based early stopping. Experimental evaluation encompasses 12 recent methods and is performed using three real-world industrial datasets. The results from both controlled offline studies and live online A/B testing corroborate the advantages of the KD-based approach recommended here.

author: Rocha
title: Cross-Layer Knowledge Distillation for Compressing Networks with Limited Data
abstract: The need to produce compact deep neural networks has led to widespread use of model compression techniques. Conventional approaches typically depend on fine-tuning that utilizes ample labeled data to maintain predictive accuracy, but such requirements may be problematic in contexts where privacy or data security concerns restrict data access. This study focuses on network compression in a scenario where only a handful of labeled instances per category are present, exploring how to achieve effective compression with minimal accuracy loss under such constraints. A principal challenge in this setting is that the reduced dataset often causes the compressed network to over-fit, which in turn leads to significant inference errors when matching the original model’s outputs. These errors tend to propagate across the network’s layers, ultimately impairing final predictions. To mitigate this issue, this work introduces a cross distillation method, which performs knowledge distillation in a layer-wise fashion. By connecting the internal representations of both teacher and student networks at each layer, this design helps to limit the accumulation of estimation errors throughout the architecture. The proposed approach is broadly applicable and can be integrated with widely-used compression strategies, including pruning. Experiments carried out on standard benchmarks reveal that cross distillation substantially enhances the performance of student models where training data is extremely scarce.

author: Ellis
title: Investigating Approaches to Representation-Based Distillation in Graph Neural Networks
abstract: The strategy of knowledge distillation facilitates the development of computationally efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) by leveraging the guidance of complex teacher networks. Previous research has introduced the Local Structure Preserving (LSP) objective, which encourages the student’s node representations to maintain the teacher’s arrangement of node relationships along the graph’s edges. In this work, we examine whether aligning the broad structural properties of node embeddings, as produced by the teacher, constitutes a superior training signal for distillation in GNNs, particularly given that practical graph data can include both hidden connectivity and unreliable edges. We describe the proposed method, which utilizes contrastive learning techniques to non-explicitly enforce the student’s node embeddings to resemble those of the teacher within a jointly defined embedding space, thereby maintaining overall graph structure. We also compile a comprehensive suite of evaluation scenarios on sizable, realistic datasets characterized by sizable disparities in performance between teacher and student GNNs. Across four benchmark datasets covering fourteen distinct and heterogeneous GNN configurations, results demonstrate that the proposed method consistently enhances the accuracy and consistency of low-resource GNN models, achieving higher scores than LSP and its alternative version that targets global structure, as well as reference methods derived from two-dimensional image recognition. Further, analysis of pairwise representational similarity between teacher and student embedding spaces indicates that the proposed contrastive approach simultaneously preserves both localized and large-scale structural features, in contrast to structure-preserving baselines, which tend to emphasize only one aspect. The implementation can be found at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

author: Baker
title: Enhancing Low-Frequency Word Translation by Optimally Utilizing Parallel Data in Non-Autoregressive Models
abstract: Synthetic training data for non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models is often created using knowledge distillation (KD). Nevertheless, this process causes inconsistencies for low-frequency terms when comparing distilled datasets to the original parallel corpora, resulting in increased prediction mistakes on these words. To address this, we incorporate pretraining to directly introduce the original data into NAT. Through examination of one-way alignments, we observed that KD enforces more deterministic matches from infrequent source words to targets, yet it lacks in establishing enough links from infrequent target words back to the source. In response, we introduce a reverse knowledge distillation step, which restores additional alignments for low-frequency words on the target side. By integrating both native and synthetic datasets in a unified training procedure, these complementary methods further augment NAT accuracy. Evaluations are performed on five standard translation datasets with two modern network architectures. The evaluation confirms that the described solution substantively and consistently boosts translation effectiveness by cutting down on the rate of low-frequency word errors. Notably, our method achieves BLEU scores of 28.2 on WMT14 English-German and 33.9 on WMT16 Romanian-English tasks. Associated code, data, and pretrained parameters can be accessed at https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT.

author: Wright
title: Knowledge Distillation Approach for Integrated Semantics, Depth, and Motion Analysis in Video Scenes
abstract: Comprehensive interpretation of environmental context is essential for autonomous agents. Prior research has demonstrated that deep neural models are able to infer depth and optical flow from single-camera video without relying on annotated supervision, as ground truth data for such tasks is often difficult to obtain. Here, we advance monocular scene understanding further by jointly learning depth, optical flow, and semantic information. For semantic supervision, we employ the outputs of a pre-trained model as distilled proxies in place of direct ground truth. Our approach consists of: (a) an original training strategy that simultaneously leverages self-supervised learning and knowledge distillation, and (b) a streamlined network design aimed at facilitating efficient computation for both high-power GPUs and power-limited embedded devices. Extensive experiments reveal that our method achieves leading performance in monocular optical flow estimation, depth prediction, and motion segmentation.

author: Hoffman
title: Knowledge Distillation in Distributed Learning with Federated Communication
abstract: In distributed learning, practitioners frequently exchange model parameters among participants instead of sharing original data. Federated learning exemplifies this by synchronizing either the gradients or weights of each model. However, this approach may incur prohibitive communication overhead, especially for modern deep neural networks characterized by a vast parameter count. To mitigate this, a strategy that communicates only model predictions, which typically have much lower dimensionality than full model states (such as 10 output classes in the MNIST example), offers a promising alternative. This chapter focuses on offering an in-depth examination of the proposed method, highlighting its potential for reducing communication costs and its relevance across differing task scenarios. The first section of the chapter delivers an asymptotic analysis rooted in neural tangent kernel (NTK) theory for two crucial knowledge transfer algorithms within this method: knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD). Following this, the chapter details a straightforward implementation in the context of classification, where empirical results are presented to compare the accuracy and communication demands of the proposed technique against those of standard federated learning. Finally, the utility of this approach is demonstrated with two application cases: deployment across wireless channels with differing uplink and downlink characteristics, and adapting the method for reinforcement learning settings.

author: Baker
title: Integrating Distinct Classifiers Using Distillation Techniques
abstract: This work addresses the challenge of combining expertise from multiple classifiers, each possessing unique model structures and non-overlapping label sets, into a unified classifier, utilizing only a general pool of unlabelled examples. The focus is on scenarios in which models trained on private data at diverse sources are available for sharing, though the original datasets themselves cannot be exchanged, often due to privacy requirements. Furthermore, individual sources may lack the data necessary to represent every class or may be constrained to certain architectures due to limited computational capacity. To resolve this, the proposed method extends knowledge distillation for the purpose of combining outputs from heterogeneous classifiers. A probabilistic connection is formulated between the predictions of these classifiers and a unified probability distribution across all potential classes. Building on this framework, two methodological families are introduced: one based on cross-entropy minimization, and another using matrix factorization. These techniques provide a means to compute soft target labels spanning all categories from unlabeled data, which then serve as substitutes for actual labels in training the collective classifier. Through comprehensive experimentation on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365, it is demonstrated that both methods clearly surpass straightforward applications of distillation, closely matching the accuracy levels of supervised classifiers trained on centralized datasets.

author: Richards
title: Text Generation through Combined Knowledge Distillation and Generative Adversarial Strategies
abstract: Natural language processing tasks including but not limited to language modeling, machine translation, and summarization rely heavily on effective text generation. In computer vision, generative adversarial networks (GANs) have established themselves as state-of-the-art in producing high-fidelity images, and have in turn prompted investigation into their application for text by NLP researchers. Nevertheless, replicating this effectiveness in language tasks is hindered by the inherently discrete composition of textual data. Here, we put forward an approach that leverages knowledge distillation to maximize the capabilities of GAN frameworks for generating text. Our method involves utilizing autoencoders (AEs) to obtain continuous encodings of sentence-level input, offering smooth probabilistic assignments to multiple words simultaneously. These encodings are then transferred via distillation for training the generator, guiding it to replicate the desirable continuous sentence representations. A series of empirical evaluations over various datasets evidence that the proposed method delivers improvements over standard GAN methods for text generation that do not incorporate pre-training, as measured by both BLEU scores and Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD).

author: Hurst
title: Compact Ranking Models with High Effectiveness via Teacher-Student Distillation for Recommendation Systems
abstract: This work introduces an approach for training ranking models, commonly applied to recommender systems, prioritizing both strong performance and computational efficiency. While knowledge distillation (KD) has demonstrated effectiveness in enhancing both accuracy and efficiency in the context of image recognition, we extend KD principles to learning-to-rank scenarios through what we refer to as the proposed method. Our approach involves having a compact student model learn to rank documents or items using standard training data, supplemented by guidance from a larger, pre-trained teacher model. The student model thus obtains ranking results closely approximating those of the teacher, while benefitting from a reduced parameter count that enables faster inference at deployment. The proposed method remains adaptable, functioning independently of the particular architectures chosen for the teacher and student ranking models. Issues unique to knowledge distillation in ranking tasks are specifically tackled. Empirical evaluation on widely-used benchmark datasets combined with leading recommendation architectures confirms that our procedure fulfills its intended goals: models trained with the proposed method occupy less than 50% of the teacher model's size, match the teacher's ranking accuracy, and consistently outperform equally-sized student models not leveraging teacher supervision.

author: Ross
title: Transferring Ensemble Knowledge via Distillation in Neural Machine Translation
abstract: In knowledge distillation, a student model is guided to higher performance by leveraging outputs from a more powerful teacher network. The inference process in Neural Machine Translation (NMT) systems is computationally intensive, and deploying a compact model can mitigate this latency. This work shows that it is possible to encapsulate the translation accuracy found in an ensemble of models or in an oracle BLEU-based teacher within a lone NMT network. Additionally, we report translation quality gains when the teacher and student share identical model architectures and parameter sizes. To address the computational demands of training student models, we propose a data selection strategy informed by teacher model outputs, which both accelerates training and enhances translation results. The described approaches are implementation-agnostic, requiring no source code modifications, and are adaptable to any NMT configuration for more efficient translation at inference.

author: Robinson
title: Analyzing and Enhancing Word Selection in Non-Autoregressive Machine Translation
abstract: Knowledge distillation plays a crucial role in the development of non-autoregressive translation (NAT) systems by utilizing the outputs of a teacher model based on an autoregressive architecture to simplify the original dataset. Our experiments indicate that this training strategy leads to the transfer of lexical choice mistakes, especially involving infrequent vocabulary, from the teacher to the NAT model. To address this concern, the proposed method incorporates the original data into the NAT training process, aiming to recover valuable details about rare words that are excluded during distillation. Specifically, the approach adds an additional Kullback-Leibler divergence objective that measures discrepancies in lexical choice between the NAT model's outputs and the choices reflected in the raw dataset. Results obtained using multiple languages and model types reveal that this technique consistently enhances the accuracy and wide applicability of NAT systems. Further analysis supports the conclusion that the method reduces errors in rare word selection, leading to measurable improvements. Notably, the approach achieves NAT performance on par with state-of-the-art models on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English benchmarks, attaining BLEU scores of 27.8 and 33.8, respectively. Source code will be made available.

author: Bright
title: Advancing Practical Lipreading via Efficient and Distilled Architectures
abstract: Although neural networks have propelled advancements in lipreading, achieving practical deployment remains challenging due to ongoing limitations in current methods. Earlier work has predominantly focused on refining architectures and increasing generalization to boost accuracy, but deployment constraints persist. The proposed method narrows this divide through several key contributions. First, using self-distillation, it achieves notable improvements on the LRW and LRW-1000 datasets, reaching accuracies of 88.5% and 46.6%, respectively, surpassing previous leading results. Next, modifications to the model’s structure are introduced, incorporating a specialized Depthwise Separable Temporal Convolutional Network (DS-TCN) head, which reduces the computational demands to a small portion compared to the already efficient baseline. Additionally, knowledge distillation is demonstrated to be a highly successful strategy for maintaining the accuracy of these compact models. Through these developments, a spectrum of models balancing accuracy and efficiency is obtained. Notably, the top-performing lightweight variants attain accuracy on the level of the best existing models, but with an 8.2-fold reduction in computation and requiring 3.9 times fewer parameters, supporting the case for bringing lipreading solutions into real-world use.

author: Hicks
title: Transferring Knowledge for Effective Domain Adaptation
abstract: Adapting to shifts between the distributions of training and test data is essential for many practical tasks. Standard Deep Learning techniques for domain adaptation typically require joint training on both source and target domain datasets. This constraint limits their practicality in contexts involving many domains, or where domains change over time, such as in spam filtering where adversarial behaviors evolve. To address these limitations, the proposed method extends Knowledge Distillation to domain adaptation settings. The approach employs multiple teacher models, leveraging their domain-specific knowledge and the relationships among their respective domains, to guide a student model. This student model is shown to attain leading performance in unsupervised domain adaptation tasks involving multiple sources, as evaluated on a widely adopted sentiment analysis dataset. In scenarios involving a single teacher, reliance solely on domain similarity does not suffice for estimating trust. Therefore, a straightforward metric is introduced, which aligns closely with teacher accuracy on the target domain. Experimental results indicate that by selecting high-confidence examples with this metric, the student model secures state-of-the-art results even in single-source transfer situations.

author: Williams
title: Adversarial Training for Data-Free Zero-Shot Distillation by Belief Alignment
abstract: Transferring knowledge from a high-capacity teacher model to a more compact student network is a widely adopted practice in deep learning. Increasing data volumes and heightened privacy concerns are making the original training data of the teacher less accessible. In this work, we introduce an approach that enables a student network to align its outputs with those of a teacher, requiring neither data nor related metadata. This is accomplished by deploying an adversarial generator, which identifies samples where the teacher and student predictions diverge most, allowing these samples to guide student training. For straightforward datasets such as SVHN, the trained student accurately mirrors the teacher's outputs, and on CIFAR10, the method surpasses previous leading techniques for few-shot distillation involving 100 examples per class, all without access to any data. Additionally, we define an evaluation metric assessing belief agreement between teacher and student close to decision boundaries, finding that the student obtained with our data-free process achieves substantially better belief alignment with the teacher when compared with a student trained on true data via distillation.

author: Rodriguez
title: A Knowledge Distillation Approach for Graph Neural Networks with Enhanced Utilization of Prior Information
abstract: Graph-based semi-supervised learning has garnered significant attention in the machine learning community. While recent advancements leveraging graph neural networks (GNNs) have produced state-of-the-art results in classification tasks, surpassing older techniques like label propagation, the intricate design of these models often results in complicated prediction processes that may overlook key prior knowledge embedded in the graph, such as the alignment of classes among structurally similar nodes. This study introduces a knowledge distillation-based approach to mitigate these limitations. The proposed method distills information from any trained GNN (serving as the teacher model) and incorporates it into a purpose-built student model. This student is constructed to integrate two straightforward predictive strategies: label propagation for encoding structure-driven knowledge, and feature transformation to capture insights from node features. Specifically, the student network combines trainable, parameter-driven modules for both label propagation and feature transformation. This design allows the student to merge knowledge distilled from GNN teachers with intrinsic prior knowledge, leading to improved inference capability. Additionally, compared to GNNs, the resulting student model offers greater transparency in its decision-making. Experiments were performed using seven GNN architectures—GCN, GAT, APPNP, SAGE, SGC, GCNII, and GLP—on five standard benchmark datasets, treating these as teacher models. The findings show that the distilled student model reliably achieves average performance gains in the range of 1.4% to 4.7% over its corresponding teacher models. Implementation details and datasets can be found at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/CPF.

author: Burton
title: Transformer-Based Large-Scale Language Modeling via Block Structure Pruning Optimized for Hardware Efficiency
abstract: Recent advances in large-scale pre-trained language models have resulted in strong performance across a range of NLP applications. Nevertheless, challenges such as limited storage capacity for weights and restricted computational throughput on various hardware devices limit their widespread use, particularly as edge computing grows in importance. This study presents a transformer-based large language representation leveraging block-structured pruning designed for compatibility with hardware requirements. Our method integrates reweighted group Lasso within block-structured pruning to achieve optimization. The technique delivers significant reductions in weight storage and computation, and yields high compression factors. Through experiments involving several architectures (BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT) on tasks from the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) suite, the proposed method demonstrates up to 5.0-fold compression while preserving accuracy or incurring only marginal losses on some tasks. Additionally, our approach can be combined with methods like knowledge distillation as used by DistilBERT, providing an extra average compression gain of 1.79-fold atop DistilBERT with no or minimal loss in accuracy. The resulting compressed models are well-suited for deployment on edge hardware platforms with tight resource constraints.

author: Conner
title: Transferring Knowledge from BERT to Simple Neural Architectures for Specific Language Tasks
abstract: The field of natural language processing has seen a progression towards neural models with increasing depth and sophistication, exemplified by recent architectures such as BERT, ELMo, and GPT. This progression has fostered a perception that older, less deep neural models are now inadequate for tasks involving language comprehension. Contrary to this notion, our work shows that minimalistic and efficient neural architectures can still reach strong performance levels without the use of extra input features, modifications to model structure, or supplementary training resources. Our approach involves using knowledge distillation to transfer information from BERT, a leading language model, into a one-layer BiLSTM, and to its siamese modification for tasks involving sentence pairs. When evaluated on various benchmarks covering paraphrase detection, sentiment analysis, and natural language inference, our distilled models deliver performance similar to that of ELMo, yet require approximately 100 times fewer parameters and provide inference roughly 15 times faster.

author: Henderson
title: Enhancing MLPs for Node Classification through GNN-Based Distillation without Graph Dependencies
abstract: While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated strong outcomes for extensive node classification tasks in graph machine learning, their applicability in industrial scenarios is hampered by scalability issues caused by reliance on data from neighboring nodes, often several hops from the node of interest. This dependence complicates inference, especially for applications sensitive to latency. Conventional approaches like pruning and quantization can decrease the number of Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations, yielding some inference acceleration for GNNs, yet these approaches do not sufficiently address the bottlenecks tied to neighbor retrieval. In contrast, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) lack any dependency on graph structure, enabling notably quicker inference, though generally at the expense of accuracy for node classification when compared to GNNs. To leverage the advantages of both architectures, this study uses knowledge distillation (KD) from GNNs to MLPs, aiming to transfer the superior accuracy of GNNs to MLPs while preserving fast inference. The distilled MLPs, referred to here as the proposed method, do not require graph information for inference. Experiments reveal that the proposed method, when tuned for accuracy, achieves inference speeds 146X to 273X faster than GNNs, and 14X to 27X faster than other acceleration strategies. In a practical production scenario covering both transductive and inductive learning over seven datasets, the proposed method enhances average accuracy by 12.36% over base MLPs and achieves parity with GNN performance on six out of seven benchmarks. Further analysis examines the situations in which the proposed method matches GNN accuracy and highlights its suitability for environments where minimizing inference latency is critical.

author: Brown
title: A Combined Approach to Reducing Vision Transformer Complexity
abstract: Recent advancements have seen vision transformers (ViTs) attract interest, as these architectures—trained with large-scale data—can match state-of-the-art results in visual tasks without using convolutional image operators. Nonetheless, the computational requirements of ViTs remain significant, primarily owing to their reliance on multiple stacked multi-head self-attention layers. Although substantial work exists regarding compression methods for convolutional neural networks, similar efforts applied to ViTs are comparatively few and generally consider only limited strategies. To address this, we introduce a comprehensive framework for compressing ViTs that integrates three main methods: pruning, skipping selected layers, and applying knowledge distillation. We present an end-to-end, budget-aware optimization approach, which simultaneously identifies model parameters, determines which layers to prune or skip, and optimizes the pruning settings for each layer, all within a distillation objective. This framework employs the primal-dual algorithm as the optimization technique. Evaluation on diverse ViT architectures, such as DeiT and T2T-ViT, using the ImageNet benchmark reveals that our method consistently achieves superior results when compared to current alternatives. For instance, in the case of DeiT-Tiny, our method reduces computational cost to half the original FLOPs with minimal or no decrease in accuracy.

author: James
title: Progressive Self-Distillation for Cross-Modal Representations under Noisy Supervision
abstract: Existing vision-language models such as CLIP utilize training objectives that inadequately manage the substantial noise and many-to-many mappings characteristic of image caption data sourced from the web, resulting in suboptimal efficiency in both computation and data utilization. Here, we present an alternative training strategy employing cross-modal contrastive learning, which integrates progressive self-distillation and adaptive, soft image-text correspondences to more efficiently learn resilient representations from noisy supervision. At each training step, the model self-distills by producing and leveraging soft alignment targets for selected image-caption pairs within the batch, which are subsequently utilized to refine the model's parameters. Across 14 standard benchmarks, our approach yields superior performance compared to the CLIP baseline in settings that include zero-shot classification, linear probing, and image-text retrieval, all without increasing computational requirements. Experiments using a robustness suite based on ImageNet distributions further demonstrate our method's improved resilience to non-i.i.d. test shifts relative to both ImageNet-trained baselines and CLIP. Moreover, scaling experiments spanning datasets ranging over two orders of magnitude indicate that the proposed approach shows increasing gains over CLIP as the number of pretraining samples grows.

author: Ferrell
title: Enhancing Supernet Optimization in Neural Architecture Search with Adaptive Alpha-Divergence
abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) employing weight sharing offers a powerful approach to streamline neural architecture development by constructing a supernet encompassing all candidate architectures as subnetworks, and training them together within this unified framework. The effectiveness of this approach depends crucially on transmitting the supernet’s knowledge effectively to the subnetworks through distillation. We observe that the standard practice of using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence for this purpose may result in student subnetworks whose estimates of the teacher supernet’s uncertainty are either too high or too low, ultimately degrading their performance. This paper introduces a strategy that leverages the more flexible alpha-divergence during supernet training, facilitating dynamic adjustment of the divergence parameter. This adaptability mitigates the tendency of subnetworks to improperly assess uncertainty relative to the teacher model. Experiments applying this alpha-divergence guided supernet training to both weight-sharing NAS and slimmable network scenarios reveal substantial performance gains. Specifically, the set of models derived via this approach surpasses state-of-the-art alternatives including BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS across various FLOPs constraints. Notably, our method attains a top-1 accuracy of 80.0% on the ImageNet benchmark with a computation budget of just 444 million FLOPs. Public release of code and pretrained models can be found at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.

author: Rice
title: Enhancing Generalization in Fake Media Detection via Continually Learned Representations and Distillation
abstract: Despite substantial advances in artificial intelligence in recent decades, progress is often constrained by dependency on static datasets and unchanging data environments. The field of continual learning investigates how AI can incrementally assimilate knowledge from ongoing sequences of related data, paralleling processes in biological learning. At the same time, the proliferation of fabricated media—including deepfakes and artificially generated facial imagery—has become a critical concern in modern multimedia applications. While several recent approaches can accurately recognize deepfakes, their effectiveness is frequently diminished due to their dependence on predetermined datasets and constrained evaluation protocols. Addressing this limitation, the present work introduces a continual learning framework for neural networks, which has the potential to offer greater data utilization efficiency. The proposed method integrates continual learning, representation learning, and knowledge distillation within a teacher-student architecture. It is constructed to handle sequential domain adaptation challenges when exposed to new collections of GAN-based synthetic faces and deepfake data, while reducing the risk of catastrophic forgetting in the student network. Through comprehensive experiments, we establish that this method achieves effective domain adaptation for detecting low-quality deepfake videos and GAN-created images on multiple datasets, surpassing established baseline techniques in this area.

author: Maddox
title: A Distillation Approach Utilizing Earth Mover's Distance for Many-to-Many Layer Correspondence in BERT Compression
abstract: Recent advances in pre-trained language models such as BERT have led to strong results across a range of natural language processing tasks. Despite these successes, the substantial memory and compute demands of such models present challenges for deployment in environments with limited resources. To address this, this work introduces a distillation technique for BERT that uses a many-to-many correspondence framework: every student network intermediate layer is trained to extract information from any intermediate layer of the teacher model. This enables the student to flexibly acquire representations from different teacher layers depending on the specific NLP task. The method employs Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) to determine the minimal cumulative cost required to transfer knowledge from the teacher to the student, facilitating effective many-to-many alignment between layers. Additionally, a cost attention module is introduced to automatically learn and assign layer weights within the EMD computation, aiming to enhance performance and speed up training convergence. Evaluations on the GLUE benchmark indicate that the proposed approach achieves results comparable to leading baselines in both predictive accuracy and compression effectiveness.

author: Valencia
title: A Review of Deep Learning Model Compression Techniques in Text Processing
abstract: Deep learning architectures such as Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, along with Transformer-based models—including Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT), Generative Pre-training Transformer (GPT-2), Multi-task Deep Neural Network (MT-DNN), Extra-Long Network (XLNet), Text-to-text Transfer Transformer (T5), T-NLG, and GShard—have driven major advances in natural language processing (NLP) and information retrieval (IR) in recent years. Despite these achievements, the large scale of these models creates challenges for deployment in real-world scenarios, which often demand reduced memory footprints, faster inference, and limited energy usage. This review examines six primary strategies—Pruning, Quantization, Knowledge Distillation, Parameter Sharing, Tensor Decomposition, and Sub-quadratic Transformer methods—that have been developed to compress these deep learning models for practical NLP applications. Addressing the pressing requirement for efficient, compact models and considering the substantial recent research output in this area, this review aims to systematically organize the contributions of the deep learning for NLP community from recent years and provide an integrated overview of the field.

author: Smith
title: Automated Approach for Compression of Generative Adversarial Networks via Architecture Search and Distillation
abstract: Growing interest in deploying Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) on portable devices for tasks including image modification, translation, and improvement has increased focus on effective GAN compression. Despite substantial progress in compressing other deep architectures, methods for reducing the size of GANs—most notably, their generators—are still in early development. Most currently available GAN compression solutions are tailored to individual architectures and particular loss formulations. Building upon advances in automated machine learning (AutoML) for model reduction, this work applies automated design to the compression of GANs, resulting in a fully automated distillation-based framework that discovers resource-efficient generator models within a custom-tailored search space. The technique employs knowledge distillation from a reference GAN to steer the search, satisfying predefined computational limits and enabling compression. This framework operates independently, does not require any pre-trained discriminators, and is broadly compatible with a range of GAN variants. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is demonstrated on two standard GAN benchmarks: super resolution and image translation. The compressed models discovered achieve significant model size reductions while delivering superior performance compared to baseline methods. Implementation code and pre-trained networks are publicly accessible at https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.

author: Le
title: Re-examining Video-Pose Representation Strategies for Activities of Daily Living Recognition
abstract: Recognizing Activities of Daily Living (ADL) has frequently relied on integrating both RGB input and 3D poses, as differentiating between similar ADL instances requires attentiveness to subtle distinctions. While recent advances in 3D ConvNets have been insufficiently flexible to parse the nuanced visual cues present in such tasks, methods jointly leveraging RGB and 3D poses have become standard. However, extraction of 3D pose data from RGB streams, especially in the absence of specialized sensors, is computationally demanding and hinders deployment in practical, low-latency environments. This raises the question: what is the optimal way to utilize 3D pose information for ADL recognition? Addressing this, we introduce an enhanced pose-driven attention framework based on a Video-Pose Network, pursuing two independent strategies. The first strategy distills pose knowledge directly into the RGB representation at the feature level; the second emulates pose-guided attention by distilling it at the attention level. These strategies are subsequently merged into a unified model, referred to here as the proposed method. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method is robust to pose noise, substantially accelerates inference, and surpasses strong baseline approaches on four widely used datasets. The approach is effective both when 3D pose input is available and when it is not. Implementation code can be found at https://github.com/srijandas07/vpnplusplus.

author: Maldonado
title: Transferring Representations by Matching Internal Features
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has been widely adopted to enable compact neural networks (students) to benefit from large models (teachers). Conventionally, these approaches employ the teacher model’s soft logits to provide additional guidance during student training. Here, we contend that aligning the intermediate features of the student to those of the teacher at the layer before output is more beneficial. This strategy not only enables direct transmission of richer representational information from the teacher’s features but is also applicable when the teacher is optimized without a softmax activation. Empirical results demonstrate that this approach surpasses established KD methods in terms of accuracy. To promote effective feature matching, we represent each feature as a combination of its norm and direction. Our analysis suggests permitting greater flexibility in the student’s feature magnitude, while concentrating on replicating the direction of the teacher’s features. To support this, we introduce a loss component derived from locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). Integration of this loss term enhances our framework’s focus on matching feature directions and reduces constraints on magnitudes, leading to state-of-the-art performance for feature-based distillation. We provide theoretical arguments for the efficacy of LSH in direction matching and broaden the scope of feature mimicking to tasks such as multi-label classification and object detection.

author: Herrera
title: Reducing Generative Adversarial Network Size through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been applied to machine learning problems including domain adaptation, high-resolution image enhancement, and producing artificial data. Leading GAN architectures typically consist of tens of millions of parameters, resulting in high computational costs and making them unsuitable for deployment on hardware with limited size, weight, and power (SWAP) constraints, such as smartphones, or in scenarios requiring immediate response. Prior research has not addressed decreasing parameter counts in GANs. In this work, we introduce an approach based on knowledge distillation: here, a compact student GAN is trained to replicate the behavior of a larger teacher GAN. Through experiments with MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A, the suggested method achieves compression rates of 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1, in that order, relative to the teacher, with no observed reduction in the fidelity of generated outputs. Experimental evidence reveals an apparent qualitative threshold in GAN compression. Further, under the constraint of equal parameter counts, GANs produced via distillation surpass those obtained through standard training in output quality. We hypothesize that this effect is due in part to the favorable optimization characteristics present in over-parameterized GANs, which are effectively trained via alternating gradient descent. Consequently, building a high-capacity GAN and then reducing its size using the introduced compression method yields a generative model of high quality with greatly reduced parameter requirements.

author: Davidson
title: Enhancing Re-Identification Robustness via Knowledge Distillation from Multiple Object Views
abstract: Many conventional Re-Identification techniques utilize tracking features in a Video-To-Video configuration to ensure robustness. Despite their effectiveness, these strategies exhibit pronounced performance losses when confronted with single image queries, such as in the Image-To-Video scenario. A line of recent research has attempted to mitigate this challenge by conveying temporal cues from networks built for videos into those designed for images. The present study introduces a novel training approach wherein knowledge distilled from a collection of perspectives of the same object serves as a richer source of supervision. In this method, knowledge from diverse visual representations is transferred within a teacher-student paradigm, with the teacher network, which has access to more views, guiding a student network that processes fewer. Empirically, this technique enables the student model to surpass the performance of its teacher as well as leading Image-To-Video approaches by significant margins—achieving improvements of 6.3% mAP on MARS, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReId, and 5% on VeRi-776. Extensive experiments are conducted on datasets for Person, Vehicle, and Animal Re-Identification to examine both qualitative and quantitative characteristics of the proposed method.

author: Rodriguez
title: Differentially Private Release of Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have seen widespread adoption in privacy-sensitive domains such as healthcare, increasing attention to the privacy risks posed by trained GNNs. In particular, even without internal access, trained GNNs remain susceptible to attacks like membership inference. This work introduces a centralized approach—referred to here as the proposed method—that enables the release of GNNs while preserving privacy. The method assumes the existence of a public, unlabeled graph, leveraging it to train GNNs with explicit privacy protections as knowledge is incorporated from both public and private sources. To achieve formal privacy assurances, the proposed method integrates knowledge distillation with random subsampling and the addition of noise to labels. A theoretical privacy analysis is conducted within the Renyi differential privacy framework. Furthermore, empirical evaluations demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves competitive results when compared to multiple adapted baselines for graph data. The implementation is publicly accessible at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

author: Graham
title: Hierarchical Auxiliary Branch Regularization in Federated Learning
abstract: Federated learning often faces obstacles due to client data being both imbalanced and heterogeneous, resulting in inconsistencies among the local networks and causing the global aggregation to converge unstably. To counter these issues, we introduce a new regularization approach that integrates several auxiliary branches into each local model. This is achieved by joining components of local subnetworks and the shared global subnetwork at multiple hierarchical positions. The main local model pathway is then trained, utilizing online knowledge distillation, to align its feature representations with those produced by the hybrid auxiliary routes. This method enhances the resilience of the global model even under non-iid data conditions and can be seamlessly incorporated into diverse federated learning setups without creating additional communication overhead. Through detailed empirical experiments, we observe substantial improvements in both accuracy and computational efficiency over prior techniques. Our implementation can be accessed from the project website.

author: Chavez
title: Knowledge Distillation Without Access to Source Data for Compressing Deep Neural Networks
abstract: Model compression techniques have recently made it possible to reduce deep neural network sizes significantly, often preserving their original accuracy. Yet, these techniques universally depend on having the training data available, which is not necessarily feasible in situations where the model was trained on enormous datasets or where privacy and safety regulations prevent dataset sharing, such as in biometric applications. In this work, we introduce a data-free knowledge distillation approach that allows deep network compression utilizing only additional metadata distributed alongside the pretrained model, removing the necessity for the original dataset. We further investigate several types of metadata suitable for integration in this framework and analyze the respective advantages and limitations presented by each.

author: Mckay
title: An Efficient Distillation Approach for Compressing Large Language Models Using Data Interpolation
abstract: Recent advances in large-scale language models have resulted in strong empirical outcomes. However, achieving these gains requires using models with increased size, greater energy demands, and slower inference, which limits their usability on devices with constrained computing or memory resources. To reduce model size, knowledge distillation (KD) has been widely adopted as a practical solution. Still, extensive neural network models frequently memorize training samples, which may lead to unstable predictions under minor shifts in the data distribution. Additionally, with scarce task-specific data, student models rarely benefit from informative guidance from their teacher counterparts. To mitigate these concerns, the proposed method introduces a distillation process independent of task data, incorporating the mixup technique for data augmentation, thus aiming to improve generalization in the distilled model. Specifically, beyond training on the original dataset, the student is also trained to reproduce the teacher’s responses to linearly interpolated input pairs. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that, contingent on reasonable assumptions, the described strategy produces a reduced difference between empirical and generalization errors. The method’s practical utility is validated on the GLUE benchmark, where it produces notable improvements compared to conventional KD and surpasses a range of strong baseline methods. Further tests in data-limited scenarios and component analysis underscore the effectiveness of this technique.

author: Liu
title: Facilitating Multimodal Generation on CLIP Using Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Large-scale pre-training approaches for vision-language dual-encoder architectures, such as CLIP, utilizing vast collections of image-text pairs, have achieved notable advances on tasks requiring multimodal correspondence. However, these models exhibit limitations in performing multimodal generative tasks, primarily due to inadequacies in their text encoders. To address this issue, this work introduces a method to enhance the dual-stream VLP model by integrating it with a pre-trained textual language model through vision-language knowledge distillation. This approach effectively imparts the ability to carry out multimodal generation, while also being markedly more efficient in terms of data usage and computational resources than pre-training models from initial randomization. Empirical findings reveal that the derived model delivers robust zero-shot results on a range of multimodal generation benchmarks, including open-domain visual question answering and automatic image captioning. Specifically, our model attains 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on the VQAv2 benchmark, outperforming the prior best zero-shot model with an order of magnitude (7 times) fewer model parameters. In addition, the process maintains the original language comprehension and generative capabilities of the pre-trained language model, rendering the resulting system adaptable for both unimodal and multimodal applications.

author: Mason
title: Student Network Training Using Feature Representation
abstract: While deep convolutional neural networks excel in many tasks, their high demands on memory and computation restrict deployment on resource-limited platforms such as mobile devices. Knowledge distillation addresses this by enhancing the efficiency of smaller student networks using the guidance of a pre-trained large teacher network. Previous teacher-student strategies frequently depended on extra fully-connected layers to link intermediate representations, inadvertently adding significant auxiliary parameters. Differing from this, our approach transfers knowledge by embedding features from teacher to student, without incorporating additional parameters that require optimization. We introduce a locality preserving loss that facilitates the alignment of low-dimensional student features with the essential characteristics found in the teacher’s high-dimensional representations. As a result, the student model is able to retain the teacher’s performance without inflating complexity. We also provide a theoretical analysis demonstrating that our method achieves reduced computational demands. Evaluations conducted on standard benchmarks and with established models indicate that our algorithm outperforms existing teacher-student approaches in terms of efficiency regarding both computation and storage.

author: White
title: Transferring Generative Adversarial Network Knowledge for Efficient Image Translation Models
abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have achieved success in image-to-image translation, yet their significant computational and memory demands limit deployment on portable devices. Existing model reduction strategies typically address visual recognition challenges, but have not been extended to generative modeling. Drawing on knowledge distillation principles, we train a student generator with a reduced number of parameters by leveraging both high-level and low-level representations from a larger, pre-trained teacher generator. To further enhance the student generator’s effectiveness, a student discriminator is introduced, which evaluates the similarity between authentic images and those produced by both student and teacher generators. This setup leads to an adversarial training scheme that jointly updates the student generator and student discriminator. Experimental results on standard datasets, including both numerical evaluations and visual inspection, indicate that this approach enables the creation of lightweight generative models with competitive performance.

author: Gaines
title: Task-aware Compression of BERT via Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
abstract: Pre-trained models like BERT have achieved strong results on various NLP tasks, yet their substantial number of parameters poses challenges for deployment in scenarios requiring fast inference and limited computational resources. Common approaches reduce BERT to more compact models, but typically apply the same compressed version to every downstream task, without adaptation. To address this limitation, the proposed method utilizes differentiable Neural Architecture Search to automatically obtain smaller BERT variants that are tailored to individual tasks. The approach introduces a loss function oriented towards task-specific knowledge distillation, guiding the search process, and integrates an efficiency-based loss to impose constraints, thereby facilitating a balance between effectiveness and resource usage in task-adaptive BERT compression. Experiments on multiple NLP benchmarks indicate that the resulting models achieve inference speeds 12.7 to 29.3 times faster and parameter counts 11.5 to 17.0 times lower than BERT, while maintaining comparable accuracy.

author: Harrell
title: Enabling Participation of All Clients in Federated Learning Across Diverse Computational Capabilities
abstract: Federated learning (FL) facilitates the collaborative training of models using decentralized data while maintaining user privacy. Conventional FL approaches typically presume that every client device can support the training of a unified global model. Contrarily, real-world FL deployments encounter a broad spectrum of device capabilities, with significant disparities in computational resources among clients. While large-scale models like BERT have demonstrated exceptional performance in artificial intelligence tasks, deploying such models in FL settings that include less capable devices presents substantial challenges. Naive approaches, such as excluding less powerful clients or enforcing a universally compact model, risk either neglecting segments of the data or compromising accuracy due to insufficient representational power. To address these limitations, this study introduces a client-inclusive federated learning strategy, referred to here as the proposed method. The principal concept is to tailor model sizes to individual clients according to their computational strengths, allocating larger architectures to robust devices and smaller ones to resource-constrained clients. Furthermore, a mechanism for mutual knowledge transfer among local models of varying capacities is developed, ensuring comprehensive participation in the training process and enabling the global aggregation of a high-capacity model. Additionally, a momentum-based knowledge distillation technique is put forward to enhance the conveyance of knowledge from large models on high-end clients to smaller models operating on low-end devices. Experimental results spanning multiple standard benchmark datasets validate that the proposed method effectively learns accurate global models in FL environments composed of heterogeneous client devices.

author: Evans
title: Distilling Efficient Evaluation Metrics for Machine Translation Across Languages
abstract: Advancements in the fields of machine translation and multilingual text generation have prompted a shift toward leveraging trained evaluation metrics—examples include BLEURT and COMET—which formulate the task as regression and utilize the embeddings provided by large-scale multilingual pre-trained models like mBERT and XLM-RoBERTa.
