However, insights from work on related problems indicate that the effectiveness of such evaluation metrics is closely tied to model scale, leading to high computational cost and reduced practicality. Focusing on RemBERT—a leading multilingual language model—and using datasets from the WMT Metrics Shared Task, we systematically examine how model size and multilingual ability interact. Through a collection of studies, we demonstrate that model capacity significantly restricts cross-lingual generalization. To address this, we introduce a distillation-based approach employing artificially created data and distributing a teacher model’s knowledge to several student models specialized in different but similar languages. This approach closes the gap caused by reduced model capacity, delivering improvements up to 10.5% relative to standard fine-tuning and attaining 92.6% of RemBERT’s performance while utilizing just one-third the number of parameters.

author: Fowler
title: Self-supervised Knowledge Transfer for Compact Visual Models
abstract: The focus of this work is on advancing self-supervised approaches for compact neural architectures. Our initial findings demonstrate that contrastive self-supervised techniques, which have delivered strong results for large-scale models, are less effective when applied to smaller networks. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a strategy in which a larger pretrained model acts as a teacher to guide the representation learning of a smaller student model through self-supervised distillation. In this framework, rather than training the student on unlabeled inputs alone, we optimize the student encoder to approximate the distribution of similarity scores that the teacher assigns to samples within a batch. Evaluations indicate that this technique leads to substantial improvements in the downstream task accuracy of small models. Specifically, on the ImageNet-1k benchmark, this approach raises the top-1 accuracy of EfficientNet-B0 from 42.2% to 67.6% and MobileNet-v3-Large from 36.3% to 68.2%, when compared to alternative self-supervised baselines.

author: Lynch
title: Distilling Visual Model Knowledge to Sensor Data for Activity Recognition
abstract: Recent advances in human activity recognition (HAR) have demonstrated that using multiple data modalities can significantly enhance classification performance. Despite this, resource constraints typical to wearable hardware, such as smartwatches, often preclude direct deployment of these complex techniques. To address this limitation, this work presents an end-to-end method for knowledge distillation from visual models to sensor-based models. Under this approach, only sensor time-series signals (specifically, accelerometer readings) are required from the wearable device for inference, thereby minimizing the computational overhead while achieving accuracy that approaches multimodal systems. The method begins by encoding the time-series signals as two-dimensional images employing the Gramian Angular Field (GAF) transformation to enable the use of visual deep learning architectures. For knowledge transfer, the teacher network is based on ResNet18, while the student is implemented as a multi-scale Temporal Relation Network (TRN) using BN-Inception. To better transfer knowledge between vision and sensor data domains, a new loss function named Distance and Angle-wise Semantic Knowledge loss (DASK) is introduced. Experiments on UTD-MHAD, MMAct, and Berkeley-MHAD datasets validate that the method is effective and competitive for HAR applications on wearable sensors.

author: Hernandez
title: Transferring Neural Radiance Field Knowledge to a Deep Neural Light Field for Faster Novel View Rendering
abstract: The rapid advancements in Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) research have demonstrated its strong capabilities in encoding detailed 3D environments using neural networks. Despite these successes, NeRF suffers from inefficient inference, necessitating hundreds of queries to its network just to generate a single pixel. While many current approaches try to mitigate this by decreasing the quantity of sample points, the necessity of repeated sampling operations persists. Contrastingly, Neural Light Field (NeLF) allows for more efficient view synthesis, as each pixel is rendered in a single forward pass, with no need for ray-marching. In this paper, a residual multilayer perceptron with 88 layers is proposed to accurately encode the neural light field. The pivotal factor for effectively training this deep NeLF is ample data, which we supply by leveraging data distillation from an already trained NeRF teacher. Comprehensive experimental results, using both artificial and real data, verify the advantages of the proposed method in comparison with existing approaches. For examples in synthetic environments, the method achieves between 26 and 35 times fewer floating-point operations per ray and 28 to 31 times faster rendering, all while substantially enhancing image quality (increasing average PSNR by 1.4–2.8 dB versus NeRF), without the need for custom parallel computation schemes.

author: Farmer
title: Enhancing 3D Object Detection Efficiency Using Knowledge Distillation Techniques
abstract: While recent advancements have improved 3D object detection, state-of-the-art 3D detectors tend to be computationally intensive. This work investigates knowledge distillation (KD) as a means to design more efficient 3D object detectors, with emphasis on commonly used pillar-based and voxel-based architectures. Given the scarcity of established teacher-student configurations in this domain, we begin by analyzing approaches to produce student networks that balance performance and resource usage, including strategies involving model size reduction and lowering input resolution. Subsequently, a comprehensive evaluation framework is developed to apply 2D knowledge distillation strategies to 3D object detection scenarios, considering six systematically constructed teacher-student pairs. Additionally, the proposed approach introduces a refined distillation method that aggregates knowledge only at select critical locations, as specified by the teacher model's classification outputs, coupled with a student initialization procedure guided by the teacher's weights for improved feature extraction transfer. Experiments on the Waymo dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of these contributions: the top-performing student achieves 65.75% LEVEL 2 mAPH, exceeding the teacher network's accuracy while consuming just 44% of its floating point operations. Furthermore, the most resource-efficient student achieves 51 FPS on an NVIDIA A100, operating at 2.2 times the speed of PointPillar and also offering superior accuracy. Implementation can be found at https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/SparseKD.

author: Ryan
title: Transferring knowledge from networks trained on multiple imaging modalities to those using a single modality for segmentation tasks
abstract: Recent research in medical image segmentation has extensively explored leveraging several imaging modalities simultaneously. Combining multiple modalities has consistently been shown to yield higher segmentation performance compared to using a single modality alone in various contexts. Nonetheless, clinical constraints such as limited access to scanners and personnel, as well as considerations of cost and scan duration, often make multi-modal acquisitions unfeasible, resulting in cases where typically only one modality is collected. This study introduces a strategy to distill knowledge from a multi-modal segmentation network (serving as the teacher) into a mono-modal segmentation network (acting as the student). Our approach adapts the general distillation paradigm to train the student on one modality by utilizing the teacher model, which was trained with several modalities as input. We provide experimental evidence on the BraTS 2018 dataset for brain tumor segmentation using multiple network architectures, demonstrating that the student model can reliably acquire information from the teacher and surpass the performance of a mono-modal baseline in segmentation accuracy.

author: Osborne
title: Transferring Representations from Deep Architectures for Improved Transparency in Computational Phenotyping
abstract: The rapid expansion of Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) data has created significant possibilities alongside pressing demands for identifying informative, data-based representations and disease patterns in Computational Phenotyping. While Deep Learning approaches yield strong results for predictive phenotyping, their lack of interpretability remains a substantial concern for clinicians tasked with making decisions. This study presents the proposed method—an interpretable modeling framework using a knowledge distillation strategy designed to extract comprehensible phenotype features that retain predictive accuracy comparable to deep learning models. Our approach leverages Gradient Boosting Trees to derive interpretable representations based on outputs from deep networks, specifically Stacked Denoising Autoencoders and Long Short-Term Memory models. Systematic evaluation using an actual clinical time-series dataset demonstrates that the proposed method matches or slightly surpasses the predictive ability of deep architectures and additionally produces phenotype features suitable for aiding clinical decisions.

author: Moreno
title: Training Neural Policies for Fast, Perception-Aware Navigation of Quadrotors Amid Obstacles
abstract: Neural approaches to control have recently surpassed traditional model-based planning and control in enabling quadrotors to traverse densely obstructed spaces as quickly as possible. Nevertheless, these policies typically lack perception awareness—an important factor in vision-guided flight, given both the restricted view of on-board cameras and quadrotors' underactuation. In this work, we introduce a learning procedure that enables agile, perception-aware quadrotor flight among obstacles. The strategy involves uniting imitation learning and reinforcement learning within a framework that grants privileged access for the instructor during training. Initially, reinforcement learning is employed to develop a teacher policy with access to the complete system state, allowing it to navigate cluttered scenarios in minimal time. Subsequently, imitation learning is applied to transfer the teacher's expertise to a student policy constrained to camera-based perception. Through close integration of sensing and control, our method achieves notably faster computations—by a factor of 10—as well as increased task success rates. Performance for closed-loop control is validated using a hardware-in-the-loop simulation platform.

author: Smith
title: Creating Compact, Efficient, and High-Performing Pretrained Language Models for Specialized Applications Through Adaptation and Distillation
abstract: The application of large-scale pre-trained models has led to notable advancements across a variety of natural language processing tasks. Nevertheless, these models encounter issues related to domain shift when utilized in specialized domains, complicating both fine-tuning procedures and real-time deployment due to limitations in latency and computational resources. This work introduces a broadly applicable technique for designing compact, high-speed, and high-quality pre-trained models tailored to particular domains. The method involves modifying general-purpose pre-trained models and employing knowledge distillation that does not depend on any specific task within the intended domain. In the adaptation phase, we incorporate an expanded domain-specific vocabulary, where the selection of the number of additional vocabulary items is determined automatically using occurrence frequencies from the domain corpus. Subsequently, we perform a detailed examination of several model reduction strategies to tailor large pre-trained models for domain-specific scenarios. Our experimental evaluation focuses on the biomedical and computer science fields. Results show that the proposed method surpasses the BERT BASE model on domain-focused tasks, with a reduction in size by a factor of 3.3 and an increase in processing speed by a factor of 5.1 relative to BERT BASE. Code and pre-trained weights can be found at https://aka.ms/adalm.

author: Nguyen
title: Applying Teacher-Student Training to Compact Highway Neural Networks for Acoustic Modeling
abstract: Recent progress in deep learning has led to notable improvements in speech recognition capabilities. Despite this, neural network acoustic models tend to be substantially larger in size than traditional Gaussian mixture models, limiting their suitability for applications on embedded systems. Earlier work explored using a more parameter-efficient highway deep neural network (HDNN), a variety of feedforward neural network that includes depth gating, for this task. Prior results indicated that HDNN acoustic models could perform at a similar level of recognition accuracy relative to standard deep neural networks (DNNs), but with considerably fewer model parameters. In this study, we extend that research by employing knowledge distillation, also referred to as teacher-student training, where a compact HDNN model is instructed using output from a high-performing, larger model. Additionally, we explore the impact of introducing sequence training and adaptation methods within the teacher-student paradigm. Experiments conducted on the AMI meeting corpus show that these techniques lead to a notable boost in HDNN model accuracy, achieving strong results with under 0.8 million parameters and reducing the performance gap relative to a standard DNN configuration with 30 million parameters.
